# If This Was a Movie

"If This Was a Movie" is a pop rock ballad by American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift . Co-written with Martin Johnson and produced by Nathan Chapman, it was originally released as a Target-exclusive bonus track on the deluxe edition of Swift's third studio album, *Speak Now*, in 2010 , . The song distinguishes itself within Swift's catalog due to its unique authorship status, as it is the only track on the album not written solely by her , . This distinction led to its re-recording being released separately from the main *Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)* album [, )]. Its critical reception has been marked by academic analysis treating it as a literary text, while its commercial history includes a record-breaking debut on the US Billboard Hot 100 . The song's enduring popularity is evidenced by its inclusion in fan polls and its thematic placement within Swift's exploration of cinematic narratives and romantic longing , .

## Composition and Release

The song "If This Was a Movie" was composed by Taylor Swift and Martin Johnson, marking a departure from the predominantly solo writing process she employed for her other works at the time , . It represents one of Swift's earliest ventures into co-writing, a practice that would become more common in her later career. The production was handled by Swift and longtime collaborator Nathan Chapman, who contributed to the song's rich, orchestral sound , . Musically, the track is characterized as a fast-paced pop rock ballad featuring a blend of acoustic and electric string instruments, drums, piano, and full orchestration, creating a dramatic and emotionally charged soundscape . The lyrics tell the story of a narrator pleading with an ex-lover who has been absent for six months, imagining a reconciliation where their relationship ends like a movie, complete with iconic tropes like rain-soaked apologies . However, the idealized cinematic ending does not materialize, highlighting a sense of unresolved longing and disappointment . The central metaphor of life unfolding like a film operates on multiple levels, including serving as a grammatical unreal conditional to express counterfactual disappointment, acting as a shorthand for romantic comedy tropes, implicitly critiquing misleading romantic narratives, and functioning as meta-commentary where the narrator critiques the disappointing finale of her own life story . One prominent lyric, "Flashback to a night when you said to me, 'Nothing's gonna change, not for me and you,'" illustrates Swift's use of involuntary memory as a potent emotional device, recalling a definitive promise that ultimately failed to hold true .

The song was initially released exclusively through Target as the sixteenth track on the Target-exclusive deluxe edition of Swift's third studio album, *Speak Now* , . The physical release occurred on October 25, 2010, via Big Machine Records , . This deluxe edition format was a common strategy at the time to offer additional value to fans and drive sales through specific retail partners . The standard 14-track edition of *Speak Now* did not include the song, which established its status as a bonus track rather than a core album piece [), ]. A significant point of clarification regarding the song's canonical placement is its frequent misassociation with Swift's second album, *Fearless*. While some analyses based on audio characteristics have categorized it within the *Fearless* era, and online commentary has suggested Swift is "trying to rewrite history" by linking the two, reliable sources consistently identify "If This Was a Movie" as a track from the *Speak Now* album , . Its thematic placement within the broader "Fearless & Speak Now: Fairy Tale Tradition" era is a valid analytical classification concerning its narrative motifs, but it is not a correct statement of its official album affiliation . The song's initial limited availability explains why its digital release came several years later. On November 8, 2011, Big Machine Records made the track available for digital download via the iTunes Store and Amazon.com as a promotional single, alongside another bonus track, "Superman" , . This digital release was pivotal, as it triggered the song's first major entry onto national charts and set the stage for its subsequent record-breaking performance .

## Re-recording and Re-release

The decision to re-record "If This Was a Movie" was directly influenced by Taylor Swift's desire to regain ownership of her master recordings, a move initiated after a dispute over the masters of her first six studio albums . As part of this extensive re-recording project, Swift announced plans to re-release her entire back catalog. However, she made a strategic curatorial choice: the primary re-recording of *Speak Now* was intended to contain only songs she had written entirely on her own [)]. Because "If This Was a Movie" features a co-writer, Martin Johnson, it was excluded from the main *Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)* album, which was released on July 7, 2023 [, , )]. This decision was necessary to adhere to her stated goal of having sole authorship credits on the primary re-recording album . Consequently, the re-recorded version, titled "If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)," was released independently on March 17, 2023 , . This date coincided with the start of her highly successful Eras Tour, and the new track was released alongside three other re-recordings timed to promote the tour , .

The re-recording was produced by Taylor Swift and Christopher Rowe, marking a shift from the original production team of Swift and Nathan Chapman , . The personnel involved in the new recording session included Amos Heller on bass, David Cook on piano, Matt Billingslea on drums, Max Bernstein on electric guitar and synthesizer programming, Mike Meadows on acoustic guitar and mandolin, and Paul Sidoti on electric guitar . The engineering and mixing team consisted of Bryce Bordone and Derek Garten as engineers, Serban Ghenea as the mixer, and Randy Merrill as the mastering engineer . The runtime of the re-recorded version is 3 minutes and 57 seconds . To market the separate release, the song was issued under Republic Records and was accompanied by the cover art from *Fearless (Taylor's Version)* [, )]. It was also included on the promotional EP *The More Fearless (Taylor’s Version) Chapter*, which helped frame the re-recording within a thematic context distinct from its original album [, )]. This deliberate separation underscores the song's unique position within Swift's discography; it is the only track on the original *Speak Now* album not solely written by her, which directly necessitated its exclusion from the main re-recording and its subsequent independent release , . This strategic divergence highlights the meticulous approach Swift took in curating both her original and re-recorded catalogs, ensuring each release met specific artistic and legal criteria.

## Critical Reception and Literary Analysis

Following its release, "If This Was a Movie" garnered significant attention from music critics and cultural commentators, who recognized it as a sophisticated example of Taylor Swift's evolving songwriting prowess. The song is often cited as a fan favorite, appearing in numerous lists of beloved tracks from the *Speak Now* era . Its lyrics, particularly the line "But I take it all back now!", have been described as iconic, encapsulating the narrator's desperate attempt to undo a past mistake and reclaim a lost relationship . Critics noted the song's departure from Swift's earlier, more straightforward narratives, situating it within a thematic cluster of 'Stories of Longing and Regret' . This group includes tracks like 'Back to December' and 'Superman', and signifies a maturation in Swift's storytelling, moving away from simplistic "villain and hero" dichotomies toward a more nuanced exploration of mutual accountability and the painful ambiguity of unresolved romantic closure . The song is positioned as a key work in Swift's artistic development, reflecting a classic coming-of-age arc where she begins to explore the complexities of faded romance and self-reflective emotional states , .

Beyond popular critique, "If This Was a Movie" has been subjected to serious academic and literary analysis, solidifying its reputation as a text worthy of scholarly engagement. A 2025 study published in *Humanitatis: Journal of Language and Literature* specifically analyzed the song's figurative language, identifying eighteen instances across ten Swift songs, including this one, and grounding its findings in Johnson & Arp's theory of figurative language . Further analysis delves into the song's intricate use of metaphor, particularly the central conceit of life as a movie. This analysis deconstructs the metaphor into four simultaneous functions: it serves as a grammatical unreal conditional expressing a counterfactual hope ("what if..."), it acts as a genre shorthand for familiar romantic comedy tropes like airport chases and rain-soaked apologies, it provides an implicit critique of the unrealistic and often misleading narratives presented in romantic films, and it functions as a form of meta-commentary where the narrator shifts from participant to critic, observing the disappointing finale of her own life story . This multi-layered interpretation elevates the song from a simple breakup ballad to a complex meditation on memory, idealization, and the gap between lived experience and cinematic fantasy .

The song's narrative framework places it firmly within the tradition of fairy tales and myths that permeate Swift's early work. It continues the trend of reframing stories of stolen love and interrupted weddings, leveraging irony and revision to subvert genre expectations . The narrator's act of remembering, particularly the involuntary flashback to a promise that has since been broken, is a recurring motif in Swift's songwriting, connecting "If This Was a Movie" to other works like 'Love Story' and 'Red' . Harvard University formally recognized the literary significance of Swift's work by offering a Spring 2024 English course titled 'Taylor Swift and Her World', taught by Professor Stephanie Burt . This course explicitly analyzes Swift's songs, including "If This Was a Movie," treating them as literary texts in dialogue with classical and modern literature . The syllabus examines themes such as adolescence, celebrity, and identity, placing Swift's narrative techniques within a broader academic context. This scholarly attention affirms the song's importance not just as a piece of popular music but as a contemporary cultural artifact that explores the human condition through the lens of cinematic yearning and romantic idealization .

## Commercial Performance and Chart History

The original version of "If This Was a Movie" achieved significant commercial success, largely driven by its digital release and the technological landscape of the music industry at the time. After its physical release on October 25, 2010, the song did not chart until it became available for digital download on November 8, 2011 , . Its debut on the US Billboard Hot 100 occurred on November 16, 2011, when it entered the chart at number 10 , . This peak position was not an isolated achievement; it was the eighth song by Taylor Swift to debut in the top 10 of the Hot 100 in the same week, making her the first artist in history to accomplish this feat . This milestone was officially confirmed by *Billboard* and was subsequently cited in Guinness World Records . The phenomenon of a concentrated, high-volume debut was made possible by the adoption of SoundScan technology by Billboard in 1991 . SoundScan replaced manual store reporting with barcode-scanner-based data collection, enabling accurate, real-time tracking of sales and fundamentally altering how chart performance was measured . Without this technological shift, such a dramatic and immediate chart entrance would have been impossible to quantify with precision .

The international chart performance of the original version was modest but notable. In Canada, the song peaked at number 17 on the Canadian Singles Top 100 chart for the week of October 31–November 6, 2010, before entering the US Hot 100 . It also charted globally, reaching number 22 on the World Singles Top 40 chart for the week of November 14–20, 2011 . However, a significant gap exists in the provided data regarding its performance on the UK Singles Chart; the song is absent from listings covering the period from 2010 to 2025, suggesting it did not chart in the United Kingdom despite its success elsewhere . This absence is notable given Swift's consistent chart-topping ability in the UK, indicating that the song's appeal may have been more concentrated within the North American market . Despite these limitations, the sustained commercial longevity of the parent album, *Speak Now*, which spent 176 weeks on the Billboard 200 chart, provides a strong backdrop of enduring popularity for the era .

The re-recorded version, "If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)", demonstrated different commercial strengths upon its release on March 17, 2023 . It debuted at number 2 on the Bubbling Under Hot 100 chart and reached number 4 on the Digital Song Sales chart with 11,300 downloads sold during its first tracking week , . Most significantly, the re-recording achieved a unique milestone on the Billboard charts. It debuted at number 1 on the Country Digital Song Sales chart for the chart dated April 1, 2023 . This accomplishment was historic, as it made "If This Was a Movie" the first composition to ever reach the number one spot on that particular chart with two distinct versions—the original had previously topped the same chart for one week in November 2011 . This dual achievement cemented the song's place in music chart history once again, showcasing its continued relevance and its broad appeal across different formats and eras of Taylor Swift's career .

## Live Performances and Cultural Impact

The live performance history of "If This Was a Movie" contains a notable point of contradiction, primarily revolving around its appearance during Taylor Swift's monumental Eras Tour, which ran from May 2023 to December 2024 . Multiple sources confirm that "If This Was a Movie (Taylor’s Version)" made its first known live debut during the tour. Specifically, it was performed as a surprise piano song at the show held in Minneapolis, Minnesota, at U.S. Bank Stadium on June 23, 2023 , . This performance marked the long-awaited return of the song to Swift's live repertoire, which had been absent since its initial release nearly a decade prior . The selection of the song for the tour's rotating acoustic set, specifically as the designated piano surprise for that date, indicates its significance to Swift and her appreciation for its connection with fans . This confirms that the song was indeed performed live, validating the existence of video evidence and fan accounts of the event.

However, this factual confirmation of a live performance is contradicted by a separate analytical source that argues the song was intentionally omitted from the Eras Tour setlist . This perspective posits that while only one song from the *Speak Now* era—specifically "Enchanted"—was included in the official retrospective, its inclusion was a highly curated and symbolic choice designed to create a "show-stopping moment" . By implication, the omission of "If This Was a Movie" suggests a deliberate curatorial judgment. The argument suggests that "Enchanted," with its overtly magical and fairytale-like qualities, was deemed a more fitting representative for the visual spectacle and narrative flow of the show, thereby elevating its symbolic importance over other potential choices , . This discrepancy between verifiable performance reports and analytical interpretations highlights the complex nature of concert retrospectives and the blurred lines between official setlists and the curated experiences presented to audiences. For the purpose of an encyclopedic article, the direct evidence of a performance in Minneapolis stands as a confirmed fact, even if the broader curatorial intent remains a matter of interpretation.

Despite the debate surrounding its tour inclusion, the song's cultural impact is undeniable. It is consistently ranked among fan-favorite tracks from the *Speak Now* era in user reviews and online discussions, often grouped alongside other popular songs like "Mine," "Enchanted," and "Last Kiss" . Its lyrical content resonates deeply with listeners, capturing the universal feeling of regret and the desire to relive moments in an idealized, cinematic fashion . The song's themes of longing, memory, and the failure of romantic narratives align it with a broader discourse on the influence of media on personal relationships, a topic that has been explored in academic settings, such as Harvard University's course on Taylor Swift's work . The song's legacy is further cemented by its inclusion in Swift's re-recording project, which has allowed a new generation of fans to engage with the track, and its historical significance in breaking chart records , . Ultimately, "If This Was a Movie" stands as a testament to Taylor Swift's skill as a storyteller, a song that has successfully transitioned from a bonus track to a celebrated and analytically significant piece of her artistic canon.

"[Ours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ours_/(song/) "Ours (song)")" Released: December 5, 2011 | _**Speak Now**_ is the third studio album by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift"). It was released on October 25, 2010, through [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"). Swift wrote the album entirely herself while [touring in 2009–2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_Tour "Fearless Tour") to reflect on her transition from adolescence to adulthood. Swift framed _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the unsaid things she wanted to deliver to the subjects of her songs. Using confessional songwriting, the album is mostly about heartbreak and reflections on broken relationships, and some tracks were inspired by Swift's rising stardom in the public eye to address her critics and adversaries. She and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)") produced _Speak Now_, which combines [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop"), [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock"), [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"), and [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop"). Its songs incorporate prominent [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") stylings, and their melodies are characterized by acoustic instruments intertwined with chiming [electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), dynamic drums, and [orchestral strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section"). After the album's release, Swift embarked on the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") from February 2011 to March 2012. The album was supported by six [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_/(music/) "Single (music)"), including the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") top-ten singles "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")", and the US [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") number ones "[Sparks Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparks_Fly_/(song/) "Sparks Fly (song)")" and "[Ours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ours_/(song/) "Ours (song)")". _Speak Now_ peaked atop the charts and received [multi-platinum certifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") in Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. In the United States, it sold one million copies within its first release week, spent six weeks at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") six-times platinum for surpassing six million [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America"). Music critics generally praised _Speak Now_ for its radio-friendly melodies and emotional engagement. Some critics thought the lyrics represented Swift's maturity in early adulthood, but several others criticized the confrontational tracks as shallow. At the [54th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "54th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2012, _Speak Now_ was nominated for [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Album "Grammy Award for Best Country Album"), and its single "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_/(song/) "Mean (song)")" won [Best Country Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Song "Grammy Award for Best Country Song") and [Best Country Solo Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Solo_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Country Solo Performance"). The album appeared in 2010s decade-end lists by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_/(magazine/) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_/(magazine/) "Spin (magazine)")_, and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked it in their lists "The 50 Greatest Female Albums of All Time" (2012) and "The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far" (2025). Following the [2019 dispute regarding the ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") of Swift's back catalog, she released the [re-recorded album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded_album "Re-recorded album") _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_/(Taylor%27s_Version/) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ in 2023, and the [master recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recording "Master recording") ownership of _Speak Now_ was acquired by Swift in 2025. [![Image 2: Taylor Swift at the 2009 VMAs, holding her trophy](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Taylor_Swift_2009_MTV_VMA.jpg/250px-Taylor_Swift_2009_MTV_VMA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taylor_Swift_2009_MTV_VMA.jpg) Swift at the [2009 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "2009 MTV Video Music Awards") [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") released hеr second studio album _[Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_/(Taylor_Swift_album/) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)")_ through [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee")\-based [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") in November 2008. The album spent 11 weeks at number one on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), the longest chart run for a female [country music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") artist.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-2) It was the best-selling album of 2009 in the United States and then-20-year-old Swift the youngest artist to have an annual best-seller since [Nielsen SoundScan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_SoundScan "Nielsen SoundScan") began tracking album sales in 1991.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-3) Two of the album's [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_/(music/) "Single (music)"), "[Love Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Story_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Love Story (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[You Belong with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Belong_with_Me "You Belong with Me")", performed well on both [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_radio "Pop radio") and brought Swift to mainstream prominence.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-4) "Love Story" was the first country song to reach number one on the [Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Songs "Pop Songs") chart and "You Belong with Me" was the first country song to top the all-genre [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_/(chart/) "Radio Songs (chart)") chart.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-6) At the [52nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "52nd Annual Grammy Awards") in February 2010, _Fearless_ won [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") and [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Album "Grammy Award for Best Country Album"), and its single "[White Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "White Horse (Taylor Swift song)")" won [Best Female Country Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Female_Country_Vocal_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Female Country Vocal Performance") and [Best Country Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Country_Song "Grammy Award for Best Country Song").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-edition.cnn.com-7) The success of _Fearless_ made Swift one of country music's biggest stars to [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_music "Crossover music") into the mainstream market.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9) At the [2009 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "2009 MTV Video Music Awards"), where Swift won [Best Female Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Video_Music_Award_for_Best_Female_Video "MTV Video Music Award for Best Female Video") for "You Belong with Me", the rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West") interrupted her acceptance speech; the incident received widespread media coverage and became known as "[Kanyegate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanyegate "Kanyegate")".[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-11) At the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards, Swift sang "You Belong with Me" and "[Rhiannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhiannon_/(song/) "Rhiannon (song)")" with [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks"); some critics commented Swift performed with weak vocals.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-12) [MTV News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_News "MTV News") commented the MTV Awards incident transformed Swift into a "bona-fide mainstream celebrity",[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-montgomery1-13) and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ said it was refreshing to see a talented singer-songwriter like Swift "make the occasional flub".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-NYTgrammy-14) Swift began writing for her third studio album immediately after she released _Fearless_ and continued during her [Fearless Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_Tour "Fearless Tour") in 2009 and 2010.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) Because of her extensive touring schedule, Swift wrote her third album alone: "I'd get my best ideas at 3:00 a.m. in Arkansas, and I didn't have a co-writer around so I would just finish it. That would happen again in New York and then again in Boston and that would happen again in Nashville."[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) Inspired by her growth into adulthood, she conceived _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the things she wanted to tell certain people she had met but never had a chance to.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) As with her songwriting on previous albums, Swift strove to convey emotional honesty with details as specifically as possible, believing it is important for a songwriter to do so.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) She described her songs as "diary entries" about her emotions that helped her navigate adulthood.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-wsj_int-17) Swift chose not to follow the trend of making increasingly sexualized music by artists of her age and believed such a path would be incongruent with her artistic vision.[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-19) ![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png) The [orchestral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestral "Orchestral") [string](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instruments "String instruments")\-laden "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")" is about Swift's confession of her wrongdoings and plea for an ex-lover's forgiveness, departing from the starry-eyed romance of her previous songs. Departing from _Fearless_'s theme of fairy tales and starry-eyed romance, _Speak Now_ explores introspection and reflections on broken relationships.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20) By avoiding sexual references in its songs, the album kept Swift's "good-girl" image intact.[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-22) Some tracks were inspired by Swift's public experience, including past relationships with high-profile celebrities, which received media attention during the album's promotional rollout.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) The confessional lyrics of _Speak Now_ are more direct and confrontational than those on Swift's past albums.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-24) On "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")", she asks an ex-lover to forgive her wrongdoings.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-25) Swift wrote the [title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_/(song/) "Speak Now (song)") after hearing a friend's ex-boyfriend was marrying another woman; in the lyrics, the protagonist crashes the ex-boyfriend's wedding and tries to halt it.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26) "[Dear John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dear_John_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Dear John (Taylor Swift song)")" narrates a devastating relationship of a 19-year-old female narrator who accuses a much-older man of manipulating her with "dark, twisted games".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Swift's encounter with an ex-lover at an awards show, where they ignored each other despite Swift feeling a need to speak to him inspired "[The Story of Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_of_Us_/(song/) "The Story of Us (song)")".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-NYmag-27) On "[Better than Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_than_Revenge "Better than Revenge")", Swift affirms vengeance against a romantic rival who is known for "the things she does on the mattress".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28) Romantic optimism is another theme of the album.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) The opening track "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" is about Swift's hope of attaining happiness despite her tendency to "run from love" to avoid heartbreak.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16) It was the first song she included on the track list because it represents her then-new perspective of romance.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-reuters-29) Swift had written "[Sparks Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparks_Fly_/(song/) "Sparks Fly (song)")"—a song about dangerous hints of love at first sight—before she released her 2006 debut album, [_Taylor Swift_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_/(album/) "Taylor Swift (album)").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-30) She re-recorded the song for _Speak Now_ after she received fan request to release it at the 2010 [CMA Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMA_Music_Festival "CMA Music Festival").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) "[Enchanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enchanted_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Enchanted (Taylor Swift song)")" describes the aftermath of an encounter with a special person without knowing whether the infatuation would be reciprocated.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) "[Haunted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haunted_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Haunted (Taylor Swift song)")" is about romantic obsession and "Last Kiss" explores the lingering feelings after a breakup.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) On "[Long Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Live_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Long Live (Taylor Swift song)")", Swift expresses gratitude to her fans and bandmates.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31) The lyrics of "Enchanted" and "Long Live" incorporate high-school-prom and fairy-tale imagery that recalls the youthful optimism of _Fearless_.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RS-32)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) [![Image 4: Kanye West performing, wearing sunglasses](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_%283378197438%29.jpg/250px-SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_%283378197438%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_/(3378197438/).jpg) The 2009 MTV Awards incident with [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West") _(pictured)_ inspired "[Innocent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innocent_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Innocent (Taylor Swift song)")". Besides love and romance, Swift wrote about self-perception. "[Never Grow Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Grow_Up "Never Grow Up")" is a contemplation of her childhood, adulthood, and future.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26) The self-aware "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Mean (Taylor Swift song)")", in which Swift sings about facing a man who had tried to take her down, was inspired by her detractors.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-34)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-35) Because of her confessional songwriting, the media became invested in Swift's personal life and believed each song is about a real person: an ex-lover, a friend, or an enemy.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-glamour-18)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Although Swift was interested to hear the response from the people to whom she dedicated the songs, she did not publicly name them and believed they would realize this themselves.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-glamour-18)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) She did reveal that Kanye West, who interrupted Swift's acceptance speech at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards, was the subject of "[Innocent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innocent_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "Innocent (Taylor Swift song)")".[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-NYmag-27) In the track, Swift sings about forgiving a man who wronged her; according to _[Esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire_/(magazine/) "Esquire (magazine)")_, the track can be interpreted as "a simple lament of a lost love, or a former friend being forgiven".[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-36) Swift wrote as many as 25 songs and by early 2010, she had begun to select songs for the album.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-reuters-29) To ensure the album would be coherent, she played the songs to her family, friends, and the producer [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"),[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) who had worked with Swift on both of her previous albums.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_release-37) Swift chose _Enchanted_ as a working title but Big Machine Records' founder [Scott Borchetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Borchetta "Scott Borchetta") recommended Swift choose a different title, deeming _Enchanted_ unfit for the album's mature perspective.[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-38) She settled on the title _Speak Now_ because she thought it best captures the album's essence: "I think it's such a metaphor, that moment where it's almost too late, and you've got to either say what it is you are feeling or deal with the consequences forever ... And this album seemed like the opportunity for me to speak now or forever hold my peace."[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Swift finalized the track list by June 2010.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16) Swift recorded much of _Speak Now_ with Chapman at his Pain in the Art Studio in Nashville.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-39) Although _Fearless_'s commercial success allowed Swift to engage a larger group of producers, she worked solely with Chapman because she believed they had a productive relationship.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-39) The recording process started with a [demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demo_/(music/) "Demo (music)"); Swift recorded vocals and played guitar, and Chapman sang background vocals and played other instruments. Initial reviews of _Speak Now_ were generally positive.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-speak_now_tops-102) On the review aggregator site [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, the album has an average score of 77 that was based on 20 reviews.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Speak_Now_2010:_Reviews-134) AnyDecentMusic? compiled 10 reviews and gave it an average score of 6.9 out of 10.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ADM-133) Most reviews approved of Swift's grown-up perspective on love and relationships.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-speak_now_tops-102) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"),[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-43) _Entertainment Weekly_,[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-51) _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")_,[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Guardian-136) the _Los Angeles Times_,[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20) and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RS-32) complimented the songs for portraying emotions with engaging narratives and vivid details. In AllMusic's review, [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine") wrote: "\[Swift\] writes from the perspective of the moment yet has the skill of a songwriter beyond her years."[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-43) _[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_ approved of Swift's self-penned material and artistic control.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28) In his consumer guide, [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") commented that although the album was too long and the romantic themes did not interest him, the songs were fascinating because of an "effort that bears a remarkable resemblance to care—that is, to caring in the best, broadest, and most emotional sense".[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Christgau-137) The album's dramatic themes of heartbreak and vengeance received mixed reviews. _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin_/(magazine/) "Spin (magazine)")_[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Spin-61) and _[Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now_/(newspaper/) "Now (newspaper)")_[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-53) said although it included some memorable tracks, _Speak Now_ was blemished by celebrity, rage, and grievances. _[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ lauded Swift's melodic songwriting for offering radio-friendly pop hooks but criticized the lyrics of "Dear John", "Mean", "Innocent", and "Better than Revenge" as shallow and shortsighted.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) According to [Steven Hyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hyden "Steven Hyden") from _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_A.V._Club "The A.V. Club")_, those tracks were _Speak Now_'s strength: "Swift's niftiest trick is being at her most likeable when she's indulging in such overt nastiness."[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Hyden-135) _Entertainment Weekly_ agreed, deeming those tracks inevitable for Swift's artistic evolution.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-51) _[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Village_Voice "The Village Voice")_ said Swift's songwriting was "not confessional, but dramatic" and found it more nuanced and mature compared to that of _Fearless_.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-58) Other reviews focused on _Speak Now_'s production. Reviews published in _Paste_[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-49) and _Slant Magazine_[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) called it a catchy album with radio-friendly pop tunes; the former was impressed by the crossover appeal but deemed the overall production dull. _The Village Voice_ took issue with Swift's vocals as weak and strained.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-58) BBC Music found the album's track list too long but called it overall a "sparky and affecting record".[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bbc_music-52) _Now_ approved of Swift's experimentation with styles other than country but considered it "too safe" and said the album was tarnished by "slickly produced power pop and a sugary sameness \[that is\] indiscernible from any number of today's radio-oriented artists".[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-53) Ann Powers appreciated _Speak Now_'s soft, introspective tracks for personalizing pop music.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20) [Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") of _The New York Times_ lauded the experimentation with genres such as blues and pop punk, and he called _Speak Now_ a bold step for Swift.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-57) On year-end lists of the best albums of 2010, _Speak Now_ was ranked 12th by _American Songwriter_ and 13th by _Rolling Stone_.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-138)[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bestsongs-139) _The New York Times_' Jon Caramanica ranked the album number two (behind [Rick Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Ross "Rick Ross")'s _[Teflon Don](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teflon_Don_/(album/) "Teflon Don (album)")_) in his 2010 year-end list.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-140) The album appeared on lists of the best country albums of 2010;
