On the 30th of May 2025, Taylor Swift announced something no one saw coming.[1](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-1-164138642)

She took to her socials to reveal that the Masters Saga is over. She has bought back the rights to everything — her music videos, her tour films, her photoshoots, but most importantly, her first six albums. In the letter posted to her website, she said:

> _“I’m trying to gather my thoughts into something coherent, but right now my mind is a slideshow. A flashback sequence of all the times I daydreamed about, wished for, and pined away for a chance to tell you this news. (…) I almost stopped thinking it could ever happen, after 20 years of having the carrot dangled and then yanked away. (…) To say this is my greatest dream come true is actually being pretty reserved about it. (…) All I’ve ever wanted was the opportunity to work hard enough to be able to one day purchase my music outright with no strings attatched, no partnership, with full autonomy. (…) Every time a new artist tells me they negotiated to own their master recordings in their record contract because of this fight, I’m reminded of how important it was for all of this to happen. (…) Thanks to you and your goodwill, teamwork, and encouragement, the best things that have ever been mine… finally actually are._
> 
> _Elated and Amazed,_
> 
> _Taylor.”_

![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7Jc-!,w_720,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3aded4b-ce21-4ab3-b72e-63ad4f11823c_4096x2732.jpeg)![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hzUT!,w_720,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6130a7fb-8ddc-48c1-ab02-96d663e5fefd_4096x2732.jpeg)

![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!WKeU!,w_720,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F688eb2e7-a69f-4412-b180-17b148b6d30e_4096x2732.jpeg)![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!pEiH!,w_720,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fce5d5fea-7214-4b27-a49c-71e0133f0364_4096x2732.jpeg)

never getting over how cute this photoshoot is. And the "You belong with me" caption? I can't.

For Swifties, they knew right away how big a deal this is. As Taylor says in her letter, she’s been fighting this fight for 20 years. Publicly, however, this battle has been ongoing since 2019, ever since her old manager, Scott Borchetta, sold his record company Big Machine Records — and thereby Taylor’s entire life’s work — to Ithaca Holdings, a company owned by record industry shark, Scooter Braun. On the 30th of June 2019, Taylor broke her silence on the deal through a lengthy Tumblr post:

> _“For years I asked, pleaded for a chance to own my work. Instead I was given an opportunity to sign back up to Big Machine Records and ‘earn’ one album back at a time, one for every new one I turned in. I walked away because I knew once I signed that contract, Scott Borchetta would sell the label, thereby selling me and my future. I had to make the excruciating choice to leave behind my past. Music I wrote on my bedroom floor and videos I dreamed up (…) I learned about Scooter Braun’s purchase of my masters as it was announced to the world. All I could think about was the incessant bullying I’d received at his hands for years. (…) My musical legacy is about to lie in the hands of someone who tried to dismantle it. This is my worst case scenario. This is what happens when you sign a deal at fifteen to someone for whom the term ‘loyalty’ is clearly just a contractual concept. (…) You deserve to own the art you make. I will always be proud of my past work. But for a healthier option, Lover will be out August 23._
> 
> _Sad and grossed out,_
> 
> _Taylor.”_

I still remember the conversations that broke out around this time. A lot of people were surprised to learn Taylor hadn’t owned the rights to her music the whole time. A lot of people, myself included, hadn’t even heard the term ‘master recording’ before. A lot of people had no clue who this Scooter Braun was, despite Taylor saying he’d been terrorising her for years.

Scooter Braun is a businessman and manager. He’s managed some pretty big acts in the past, most notably Justin Beiber, Kanye West, Ariana Grande, and Demi Lovato. As Taylor mentions in her post, he played a role in Kanye West’s _Famous_ music video, which disgustingly includes a naked wax figure of Taylor. So yes, Scott Borchetta knew Taylor would be upset when he sold her masters to Scooter. Of all the people he could’ve sold them to, he sold them to Scooter _because_ he knew it would hurt Taylor the most. Taylor signed a 13 year contract with Scott and Big Machine when she was 15 years old. It baffles me that so many people still say it’s her own fault she didn’t read the contract carefully. She was 15. She was just excited to be getting a record deal.

After a lot of messy back and forth for a few months in 2019, Taylor confirmed in an interview she had every intention of re-recording, but she legally had to wait until November of 2020 to make a start on the first five, and November of 2022 for the most recent, _Reputation._ In November of 2019, there was more chaos when Taylor again took to Tumblr to inform everyone that Scott and Scooter were blocking her from using her old music in her upcoming AMAs Artist of the Decade performance _and_ her upcoming documentary, _Miss Americana_. In the statement, she tells her fans to, “please let Scott Borchetta and Scooter Braun know how you feel about this” (she was funny for that, ngl). Big Machine denied this, and Taylor eventually did get to include her old catalogue.

In April of 2020, Big Machine released an EP onto streaming services of old unreleased live performances by Taylor. Taylor took to socials to say she was not made aware of this, and asked fans not to stream. In November of 2020, Taylor released yet another statement saying her team had attempted to go into negotiations with Scooter’s company, but his team refused to talk business in any way until Taylor signed an NDA (Non Disclosure Agreement) declaring she would no longer say anything negative about Scooter Braun publicly. Taylor refused. It was also in late 2020 that Scooter sold Taylor’s masters to Shamrock Holdings, but in a deal that ensured for a period of time, Scooter would still make profit off the music. Shamrock reached out to Taylor in hopes of being on good terms with her, but Taylor didn’t want any involvement with them if they were still involved with Scooter.

The master recording of a song is essentially the finished, recorded track. It is the version that is released onto streaming services and pressed onto vinyl. It is the version you hear on the radio or in the supermarket. But while Scooter and Shamrock owned the master recordings, Taylor, as the songwriter and creator, still owned the composition. Owning the composition of a song provides an artist with certain rights, including the ability to re-record. When Taylor set out to re-record, she had two aims. Yes, she wanted to finally own her old music. But she was also a woman on a mission to devalue the ones that Scooter owned, and make him regret ever buying them in the first place. Many thought there was no way she was going to succeed. Even if she could recreate them half decently, she could never convince people to listen to the new versions. She wanted to prove those people wrong.

And that she did.

![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-5uC!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0a9f9ee4-a4eb-489f-869e-34df03a153a6_600x600.jpeg)![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zAma!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F791670e1-e3ed-4090-9b61-a3782fa3401d_1400x1400.png)![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2aIG!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0d39d89b-2cd7-4a9b-b1e8-fcb19fc01cd2_600x600.jpeg)

In December of 2020, we got to hear the first snippet of any re-recording. The re-recorded verison of _Love Story_ was included in a Match.com advertisement. This would become a recurring theme throughout the re-recordings; Taylor would repeatedly use snippets of the new versions in TV shows, trailers, and ads. It became her way of giving fans a sneak peak. On the 12th of February 2021, Taylor announced _Fearless_ would be her first re-record. It would be titled _Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_, and _Love Story (Taylor’s Version)_ would be out at midnight.

This was shocking for fans because most of us assumed she would be releasing the re-recorded albums in the same order the original albums were released. I remember being shocked at the time because it hadn’t even occured to me she could release them in an order of her own choosing. In hindsight, it was a smart move, because it added an air of mystery and surprise to the project as fans were always speculating and theorising over which record was coming next. Before this annoucement, there was also a lot of discussion as to what she would be calling these re-records. Again, calling them (Taylor’s Version) was clever. It made the project feel more personal than if she had referred to them as re-records or remakes.

With this announcement also came the confirmation of the vault tracks. Many fans correctly guessed these re-recordings would include a set of songs that, for whatever reason, didn’t make the album the first time around. It was no secret Taylor was sitting on a treasure trove of unreleased songs; dozens of her demos had leaked online over the years. Again, it was a really smart way to draw people into a project they otherwise might not care about. Plenty of casual fans wouldn’t care to sit and listen to an album they’ve basically already heard before, but the intrigue of songs that are old and new at the same time? Songs that were written by young Taylor years ago and are only just now seeing the light of day? I’m going to be completely honest, the re-recordings wouldn’t have been nearly as interesting if not for the vault tracks.

Many were also wondering how Taylor would go about the album covers for these projects. I remember hearing she couldn’t do a complete recreation of the original photo, otherwise she’d be at risk of copyright (although I’m not 100% sure that’s true). If I’m honest, of all the Taylor’s Version covers, _Fearless_ is my least favourite. I love the original _Fearless_ cover, with her iconic signature curls. I think I’d like the _Fearless TV_ cover more if it didn’t have that strange browny yellow filter over it. I wish the filter was more of a light golden and more subtle. But I do like the fact that she’s turning her head the opposite way; that symbolism feels intentional.

Every single one of Taylor’s albums includes a foreword where she provides some futher context to the album, and the re-recordings were no exception. In the _Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_ foreword, Taylor reflects on the original era, stating: “It was a real honour to get to be a teenager alongside you. And for those of you I’ve come to know more recently than 2008, I am ecstatic that I’ll get to experience a bit of that feeling with you in the very near future. Now that I can fully appreciate it in its whimsical, effervescent, chaotic entierty. _Fearless_ was an album full of magic and curiousity, the bliss and devestation of youth. It was the diary of the adventures and explorations of a teenage girl who was learning tiny lessons with every new crack in the facade of the fairytale ending she’d been shown in the movies.”

_Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_ came out April 9th 2021. Out of the four re-recordings we have received, I still assert that _Fearless_ is simultaneously the one that is most faithful to the original and the one with the most improvements. This is an opinion that many seem to hold, based on the much time I have spent lurking in Swiftie spaces. Take, for example, the title track, _Fearless_. Even with Taylor owning the original now, I will never revert back to it. On the new version, the production is crisper and more hard-hitting, the vocals are so much richer and stronger, and the mixing is better too. _Fearless_ went from being a song that I was almost indifferent to, to a song that is deeply special to me.[2](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-2-164138642)

There are multiple other songs that had a similar effect. _Hey Stephen_ and _The Way I Loved You_ are two songs that benefit a crazy amount from updated production and richer vocals. _Hey Stephen_ was a song I saw in a whole new light after the re-recording, and while I’ve always recognised _The Way I Loved You_ as the goated song it is, I somehow fell even more in love with it after the Taylor’s Version. Many of the platinum tracks were improved, like _Jump Then Fall_ and _Come in With the Rain_. But easily the biggest glow up of the entire project is the platinum track, _The Other Side of the Door_.

_The Other Side of the Door_ was a song I did not care about before _Fearless TV_. And I wasn’t alone in that. It wasn’t a song I ever heard anyone really talk about. I don’t know what was in the air that day when Taylor went into the booth to record the new version, but oh boy, I’m glad it was there. I think it’s abundantly clear that in 2009, 19-year-old Taylor simply didn’t have the vocal ability to sing the song with the perfect delivery and cadence she wanted to. But 31-year-old Taylor, who’d had proper training and years to develop her voice, was able to.

That was the biggest difference people noticed at the time: _Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_ really highlighted how much Taylor’s singing had improved over the years. When Taylor recorded the original version of _Fearless_, it was before she had done any real training for her voice. So many of the songs, like _Breathe_ and _Tell Me Why,_ benefited greatly from richer vocals. In full honesty, I don’t think there’s any botches on _Fearless TV_. In saying that, there are still a couple songs where I will be returning to the original version.

Firstly, _Fifteen_. I always found the original version of _Fifteen_ funny. It’s an 18-year-old singing a song about an age she was 3 years prior, acting like she’s gained all the wisdom in the world in that short time. Really, it’s a song that makes more sense when it’s sung by a 30-year-old who actually _has_ gained wisdom. Nonetheless, there is an emotion captured in the original _Fifteen_ that I don’t feel in the re-record. The original _Fifteen_ is so nostalgic to me, and the nostalgia is amplified by Taylor’s younger vocals.

_You’re Not Sorry_ and _Untouchable_ were always two of my favourites from _Fearless_, but I found myself falling out of love with those songs while listening to the Taylor’s Versions. Now that I’m listening to the original versions again, I’ve been reminded why I loved those songs in the first place. I don’t think there’s anything particularly wrong with or bad about those Taylor’s Versions, but for me personally, they just don’t hit the same. Specifically with _Untouchable,_ I feel as if the Taylor’s Version doesn’t capture the same magical airiness in the production.

I think _Love Story (Taylor’s Version)_ is so much better than the original, but that’s one where I’ve included both the OG and the TV in my playlist; same with _You Belong With Me_. Sometimes I want to listen to the updated versions with better production and better vocals, and sometimes I want to listen to the nostalgic versions with Taylor’s baby voice.[3](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-3-164138642)

While most agree _Fearless_ is the most faithful re-recording, simultaneously the general consensus is that it has the worst vault. The vault starts on an unbelievable high with _You All Over Me_ and _Mr Perfectly Fine_, but that is also where it peaks. It’s come to my attention that most fans don’t care for _You All Over Me_ and find it boring. Couldn’t be me. I love that song. It is one of my favourite vault tracks across all the re-records. I love the gentle guitar; the harmonica; Taylor’s smooth vocals. Marren Morris’ vocals are subtle, but blend well with Taylor’s. I also love the story told in the lyrics. In conclusion, if you think this song is boring: You’re wrong.[4](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-4-164138642)

But of course, I’ll concur that _Mr Perfectly Fine_ is the crown jewel of the _Fearless_ vault. This song is basically just 4 minutes and 37 seconds of Joe Jonas slander, and it’s beautiful. In this song, Taylor is calling her ex out on his pretentious attitude and empty promises. _“How’s your heart after breaking mine?”_ is such a simple yet effective line. I think the reason why this song was left off the original album is pretty obvious: it’s too pop. Even if you threw in a banjo and a southern drawl, the melody is far too pop for it to be country-converted.

[![Image 9: @taylorswift13's video Tweet](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q08p!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9fc90c86-8f2f-4542-bb85-53277cdf602f_1200x675.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q08p!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9fc90c86-8f2f-4542-bb85-53277cdf602f_1200x675.jpeg)

the literal Fearless vault

This is when the _Fearless_ vault unfortunately takes a turn for the worse. _We Were Happy_ does have some things going for it. I like the concept: it’s a bittersweet song reminiscing on a time now past in a relationship when they were happy. Just because it ended in heartbreak, doesn’t mean the happiness gets erased. However, Taylor has a much better song about this concept, namely, _happiness_ on _evermore_. The chorus and bridge are nice, but I find the verses boring. I also find the lyrics to be rather surface-level; I wish they were more detailed. I just never find myself revisiting this song.

_That’s When_ is very mediocre to me. There’s nothing particularly bad about it, but there’s nothing particularly good about it either. And sometimes boring is worse than bad. Again, it’s a nice concept, but there’s no grit to the lyrics. Keith Urban doesn’t add much either. _Don’t You_ I like a little more. There’s a little more to dissect in the lyrics. But do I find myself revisiting it often? Not really. _Bye Bye Baby_ is an interesting one for me. When I first heard it, I absolutely loved it. It was actually my favourite from the vault for a while. But as time wore on, it lost some of its sparkle. I still really like it, but I don’t love it as much as I used to. However, I am still scandalised Taylor never performed it at all as a surprise song on the Eras Tour.

For the most part, I understand why songs like _We Were Happy, That’s When_ and _Don’t You_ didn’t make the cut for the original album. It’s because they’re not better than any songs on the original. Also, we know for a fact that _That’s When, You All Over Me, Don’t You,_ and _Bye Bye Baby_ (originally called “One Thing”) were actually written in 2005, before her debut album had even come out. So really, _Mr Perfectly Fine_ is the only true _Fearless_ vault track. To be honest, I think most of the leftovers from the _Fearless_ writing sessions she’d already used for the platinum tracks, which is why she had to reach real deep into the abyss of unreleased songs to make up that vault.

I often feel as if _Fearless TV_ felt like the least like an era because it came first. It was the trial and error re-recording, because she didn’t yet know how much people would care. It hardly got any promotion, it certainly didn’t get a music video, it didn’t even get a proper photoshoot. But once Taylor realised how much people cared, she fleshed the other re-recordings out more. _Fearless_ was the scapegoat in that sense. Despite a hit and miss vault, _Fearless (Taylor’s Version)_ still does an incredible job of recapturing the magic of the original album.

![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qO4w!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdb95898c-75b4-470f-816d-221797882f49_600x600.jpeg)![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OobW!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca2474a0-bb1e-4f72-898c-0b72c02cfe68_1400x1400.png)![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Ztwt!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff81013e2-d640-488d-afa2-d5e8eab3801e_600x600.jpeg)

In June, only several months after _Fearless TV_, Taylor started dropping hints that _1989_ would be the next album to get the re-record treatment. So naturally, Swifties started going crazy with theories and speculation and even pretended to release 1989 (Swiftie’s Version).[5](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-5-164138642) Which is why, on the 19th of June 2021, fans were gobsmacked when Taylor announced the next re-recording would actually be _Red_. It was set to be released on the 19th of November, although the date eventually got pushed to November 12th to make room for Adele’s _30_.

This announcement was very confusing. For starters, she announced it five months in advance. Even for a regular album cycle, that’s a long wait. Secondly, she had genuinely been hinting towards _1989,_ we’d even already heard a snippet of _Wildest Dreams_, which led many fans to theorise she _had_ intended for that to be the next re-record, but the _[Shake it Off](https://variety.com/2022/music/news/taylor-swift-shake-it-off-lawsuit-dropped-1235458220/)_ [songwriting credits lawsuit](https://variety.com/2022/music/news/taylor-swift-shake-it-off-lawsuit-dropped-1235458220/) pushed it back. Nonetheless, fans were still delighted to be receiving _Red (Taylor’s Version)_ and in her annoucement post, Taylor chaotically ended it with, “this will be the first time you hear all 30 songs that were meant to go on Red. And hey, one of them is even 10 minutes long.”

This was pandemonium. The supposed 10 minute version of _All Too Well_ was a huge part of Swiftie lore and legend. It was always said that the original demo of _All Too Well_ was around 10 minutes long, before Taylor and her co-writer, Liz Rose, cut it down to the 5 minute version we all know and love today. For years, fans would beg Taylor to release the full uncut version. But for a while, it seemed Taylor herself didn’t even know where it was, even once joking it was lost in a drawer somewhere. At the time, Taylor’s label never would’ve let her put out a 10 minute song. Now, there was nothing stopping her. Fans were ecstatic to learn we were finally getting the fabled 10 minute version.

I remember at the time a lot of people didn’t like the new cover, but I’ve always loved the _Red TV_ cover. In the original cover, most of Taylor’s face is concealed by a shadow from her bowler hat, with the accentuated focus of the photo being her iconic red lip. In the new cover, she’s in a gorgeous vintage car, backdropped by a forestry landscape. She’s wearing a big beige coat while showing off her Red ring.[6](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-6-164138642) Her newsboy cap is still casting a shadow over her face, but more of her features are visible; she’s older, she’s wiser, and she’s healed from this heartbreak. Most importantly, her iconic red lip is still the central focus of the photo.

In the album foreword, Taylor shed some light on how she views _Red_ now, saying: “Musically and lyrically, _Red_ resembled a heartbroken person. It was all over the place, a fractured mosaic of feelings that somehow all fit together in the end. Happy, free, confused, lonely, devastated, euphoric, wild, and tortured by memories past.”

_Red’s_ recreation wasn’t as flawless as _Fearless_, but let’s start with what she did right. The album starts off strong with impeccable re-recordings of _State of Grace_ and the title track, _Red_. Those two songs experienced such an update in production. There are some random deep cuts I feel are better than the original, namely, _I Almost Do, Stay, Stay, Stay, The Lucky One,_ and _Begin Again_. There are quite a few songs I feel are inbetween, where they’re neither better nor worse than the original.

For example, I’ve added both versions of _Treacherous_ and _Sad Beautiful Tragic_ to my playlist because I feel both have something different to offer. Taylor retroactively added _Safe & Sound_ and _Eyes Open_ to _Red_ in 2023, which are the two songs she wrote for the Hunger Games soundtrack. These two songs I absolutely adore, and I’ve added both versions of the songs to my playlist, because both the TVs and the OGs are incredible. Taylor also added _Ronan_ among the new collection of _Red_ songs, and the re-recorded version is just as touching and heartbreaking as the original.

Now let’s talk about the Max Martin of it all. Famously, one aspect of _Red_ that made it stand out from the rest of Taylor’s discography was that she branched out to work with new producers for the first time. For her first three records, Taylor worked almost exclusively with the one producer, Nathan Chapman. The three biggest hits from _Red_, however — _We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together, I Knew You Were Trouble,_ and _22_ — were produced by pop production legend, Max Martin (& Shellback). Max Martin is responsible for some of the biggest pop songs of all time: Brittany Spears’ _Baby One More Time_, Backstreet Boys’ _I Want it That Way_, NSYNC’s _It’s Gonna Be Me_, The Weeknd’s _Blinding Lights_, not to mention most of Katy Perry’s and Ariana Grande’s hits.

No one knows why he didn’t come back for any of the re-recordings. But his absense was noticeable. I still so vividly remember sitting on my bed, listening to _Red TV_ for the first time, getting to _I Knew You Were Trouble_, and physically cringing when I heard the drop in the new version. I still can’t quite place why it just doesn’t sound right. The more I’ve listened, the more I’ve adjusted to the TV, but the original IKYWT still leaves the Taylor’s Version in the dust. But the biggest crime committed is easily _We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together TV_. Obviously, the worst part is the “weeEEE” falling flat in the chorus, but overall, the energy of the entire song falls flat.

In the original version, Taylor is singing with so much spite and snark in her voice. In the Taylor’s Version, she just sounds… bored. I get it. She’s sung that song live hundreds of times at this point. I hate to be nit-picky, but I will: I don’t like the different sounding guitar, I don’t like the squeak in Taylor’s voice in the bridge, I don’t like that she exhales through her nose instead of properly sighing in the iconic spoken word part. As for _22 TV_, I personally don’t see what’s wrong with it. I like both versions of that song.

But the Max Martin songs aren’t the only bungles. The production and energy on the original _Holy Ground_ hits so much harder. The guitar and percussion have less of a kick on the Taylor’s Version. It also feels slower somehow. Secondly, I hate _Starlight (Taylor’s Version)_. The verses are fine, but the chorus feels clunky. But to be honest, it’s never bothered me that much because _Starlight_ is far from being a favourite of mine. On _Everything Has Changed (Taylor’s Version)_, it’s obvious Ed is struggling to hit some of those high notes, especially in the bridge. There’s nothing offensively wrong with _The Moment I Knew (Taylor’s Version)_, but the production is so much cleaner on the original.

But easily the most different re-recording across the entire project is _Girl at Home_. I’ve always been a part of the 1% of Swifties who actually like this song. Is the messaging of it a little sus? Yes. But it’s not as bad as everyone makes it out to be. While for the other re-recordings, it was apparent Taylor was trying to be as faithful to the original as possible, for this song, she completely changed the production. She changed it from a mostly acoustic guitar track, to a synth-heavy dance pop banger. At first, I hated this new version. I think I was just scared this meant she was going to change other re-recordings. But now, I’m actually obsessed with the Taylor’s Version of this song. The drop in the chorus has no right hitting as much as it does.

There’s probably a myriad of reasons why Taylor changed _Girl at Home_ as much as she did. Firstly, I think Taylor is aware of what Swifties think of each of her songs. She knows what songs are the fan favourites (hence her special treatment of songs like _august, Getaway Car, Enchanted, All Too Well, Cruel Summer_, etc.) and she knows which songs fans make fun of (there’s a reason _ME!_ didn’t make the Eras Tour setlist). Secondly, I’ve heard that the original _Girl at Home_ was only ever a demo. I can see this being true, as there’s something about the production in the original that sounds half-baked. Maybe Taylor always wanted the song to sound more like that.

While _Red_ has more fumbled re-recorded songs than _Fearless_, it makes up for that with its incredible vault, though that’s not to say I’m a fan of every track. _Red_ easily has the longest vault, with 9 songs. The vault opens with a song we’ve heard before, _Better Man_. _Better Man_ was a song Taylor originally wrote for _Red_, but she gave it to the country band Little Big Town in 2017. _Better Man_ is one of my all-time favourite Taylor Swift songs. The lyrics, the melody, the strings; it’s all gorgeous. I used to listen to the Little Big Town version constantly. I would have cut off my right arm for an official version of the song sung by Taylor. I could never understand why she cut such an incredible song from the album. How did songs like _I Almost Do, Stay, Stay, Stay,_ and _Starlight_ make the cut, when _Better Man_ was right there? Luckily, my prayers were answered with this vault track. And I didn’t even have to cut off my right arm for it.

Another vault high is _Nothing New_, featuring Phoebe Bridgers. Phoebe is one of my favourite artists, and _Punisher_ is one of my all-time favourite albums. I remember back in 2021, Phoebe actually getting a verse on this song was a big deal. Swifties couldn’t help noticing whenever Taylor had a female artist featuring on one of her songs, they would only ever sing backup vocals. Whereas whenever she did a feature with a male artist, they would always get an entire verse. Taylor clearly heard that and listened.

This is such a sad song. Taylor was only 22, and yet she already felt as if she were old news. She already felt as if her career was fizzling away as people were slowly losing interest in her. _“How can a person know everything at 18, but nothing at 22?”_ is such a stellar line. I completely understand why it was left off the album, however. I don’t think a song like this would’ve been received well in 2012; it would have been perceived as complaining. Also, the _“I’ve had too much to drink tonight”_ line would never have seen the light of day back then, not when Taylor was still in the throes of her good girl persona.

The next vault song is yet another one we’d heard before, _Babe_. Like _Better Man_, Taylor gave this song away in 2018 to a country band called Sugarland, although Taylor does backup vocals on their version. I think Taylor’s version of this song is infinitely better, even though she popified it. The horns add a lot, as do the little _“what about your promises, promises?”_. Then we have what is, in my opinion, the first miss of the vault. At first, I found _Message in a Bottle_ to be a cute little bop that sounds straight out of a romcom. But over the years, I have found myself pressing the skip button every time I hear those opening beep boops. In full honesty, I now find the song annoying. Something about it just gets under my skin.

But we get right back on track with _I Bet You Think About Me_, with Chris Stapleton. The joy I felt hearing Taylor exaggerate a fake country accent in a song again was unparalleled. The level of Jake Gyllenhaal hateration on this song is insane. She called him out on his hipster bullshit. I also love the music video, which was directed by Blake Lively. Taylor serves so many looks in the video, in particular the wedding dress is absolutely jaw-droppingly gorgeous. I love the concept of Taylor haunting her ex even on his wedding day, and the way that’s highlighted through every other person wearing white except Taylor in her aggressively red outfits.

_Forever Winter_ is a song I’ve listened to the whole way through only once because it hits too close to home, so I’m really not qualified to give an opinion on whether it’s good or not. _Run_ is another collaboration with Ed Sheeran, the first song she wrote with him. I want to like this song, but I mostly find it criminally boring. I like the concept of skipping town with your lover and there are some lines I like, but overall, this song just doesn’t do it for me. I know _The Very First Night_ is a beloved song for many, and the hook is catchy, but I don’t find myself revisiting it often. I know it’s petty, but I’m still not over her saying, “didn’t read the note on the polaroid picture, they don’t know how much I miss _you_,” when the rhyme of “how much I miss _ya_,” was right there.

Finally, we have made it to the vault song of all vault songs: _All Too Well (10 Minute Version)_. I still so vividly remember listening to it for the first time. I had an out-of-body experience. The newly added sections add so much to the story. She makes references to so many other songs on the album, adding a layer of interconnectedness not present on the five minute track. You can’t fully understand this song without first listening to the rest of the album, which is why its placement as the final track of 30 is so perfect. At first, I was slightly annoyed by the less intense production. The way the original version builds with those drums is so cathartic. But I think the more muted production in the 10 minute version is intentional so that the listener can really pay attention to the lyrics.

There’s a lot of debate about whether this version is actually the original 10 minute version from 2011. This is something I go back and forth on. I think most of it certainly was written in 2011. But there are also some lines I think Taylor added in 2021. For example, you’ll never be able to convince me that “fuck the patriarchy” was written in 2011. I’m sorry, but the Taylor who had only just written _Better Than Revenge_ didn’t know what the patriarchy was. Everyone knows Taylor didn’t have her feminist awakening until 2014. I also don’t think, _“I’ll get older but your lovers stay my age,”_ was written in 2011.

And of course, in addition to the 10 minute version of _All Too Well_, we also received the _All Too Well_ short film, written and directed by Taylor. Overall, I like the film, but I do have my qualms with it. First of all, it’s beautifully shot. Filming it on 35mm adds a lot to the aesthetic and ambiance. Dylan and Sadie do incredible jobs as their respective characters. Sadie does an amazing job capturing the essense of young Taylor, and Dylan does an amazing job acting as a manipulative asshole who is simultaenously charismatic. The film definitely depicts how much of a whirlwind romance this was; how one moment they’d be laughing and dancing and lost in their little love bubble, then the next moment they’d get into a screaming match where he’d belittle her and make her feel so small.

I go back and forth on how I feel about the fight scene. Taylor has stated many times the scene was improvised, which I think is noticeable. Some of the lines feel awkward or clunky, especially from Dylan. Overall, however, the fight scene portrays exactly what it needed to: How manipulative Dylan’s character is. Although I do wish we had gotten more talking scenes so it felt more like a short film and less like a music video. The scene of Sadie laying on her bed sobbing her eyes out after the breakup is forever ingrained in my brain, as is the ending. I love the symbolism of the ending; how in the short film, she took her pain and used it to write a book, much like Taylor in real life took her pain and used it to write an album.

Out of all the re-recordings, _Red (Taylor’s Version)_ was definitely the most of an era. Because of the short film, Taylor did so much promotion. We got late-night interview appearances and SNL performances for the first time in years. This was also around the time when Taylor started to get the recognition of a great lyricist and songwriter she deserved. Yes, she was always commercially successful, but people still diminished her artistry constantly. After _folklore, evermore,_ and _Red TV_ (especially after _All Too Well 10_), Taylor had a whole new wave of fans and admirers wash in. I distinctly remember that _Red TV_ is the last time the fandom felt _small_.[7](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-7-164138642) Depsite not being the perfect re-recording, and _Red_ being far from my favourite Taylor album, I look back on this era very fondly.

![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jjvi!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F75be6192-2fc3-4fee-8fbd-daabd09d9102_600x600.jpeg)![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1knU!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1509361d-86bc-427c-907c-fc9408489228_1400x1400.png)![Image 15](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q_Sh!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe08e8b0-c77c-458b-9259-e24a401f33a9_600x600.jpeg)

Throughout the first half of 2022, Taylor was radio silent. Fans were confused. Where was the next re-recording? Surely Taylor would want to get the re-recordings out of the way as soon as possible? At the VMAs in August, while accepting the award for Video of the Year, Taylor took to the stage to announce that her brand new 10th studio album, _Midnights_, would be coming in October.

This was shocking, because most fans assumed Taylor wouldn’t be releasing any new music until the re-recording project had been concluded. I don’t know how Taylor had the time to write and record 22 new songs on top of re-recording her old work, while also planning and preparing for a stadium tour, but this is when we were in the thick of Taylor’s hyper-productive era. On the 5th of May 2023, during the surprise song set of Taylor’s first Eras show in Nashville, the home of country music, Taylor addressed the audience, saying, “rather than me _speaking_ about it, I thought I would just show you.” The screen then revealed the cover for _Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)_, which dropped on July 7th 2023, well over a year after _Red_.

Of all the Taylor’s Version covers, _Speak Now_ is my favourite. The fairytale princess aesthetic was a big part of the original _Speak Now_ era. Big, fluffy ball gowns were a staple part of that album’s outifts, both on tour and in the photoshoot. In the TV cover, she’s wearing a giant layered dark purple gown. She’s styled her hair back into those iconic ringlet curls. I love that she didn’t do a white backdrop like the original, instead opting for a darker background. Again, it feels symbolic; she’s older, she’s wiser, she’s less innocent and naive. Of all the re-recordings, _Speak Now_ has the best photoshoot. Those ballet slippers and flowy dresses fit the vibe of the album perfectly.

_Speak Now_ also has the most honest and personal foreword of all the re-recordings. Which is fitting, because of her first six albums, _Speak Now_, is undoubtedly the most honest and personal. In it, she touches on the weirdness of growing up and being a teenager while famous. She touches on how the public scrutiny she faced shaped her decision to write the album completely self-written. She says: “This period of time is so violently aglow with the last light of the setting sun of my childhood (…) it was an album that was most precious to me because of its vast extremes. It was unfiltered and potent.”

The re-recorded _Speak Now_ tracks are interesting for me, because most of them aren’t bad, per se, but I majoritively prefer the originals because of the nostalgia. _Mine, The Story of Us,_ and _Innocent_ benefit from updated production and vocals. _Back to December, Speak Now,_ and _Ours_ are examples of songs where the Taylor’s Versions aren’t bad, I just prefer the originals because of the nostalgia. Other than _Ours_, the Taylor’s Versions of the other deluxe tracks are better. _Superman_ is one of Taylor’s least popular songs, but I adore it. And despite Taylor trying to rewrite history and make us think _If This Was a Movie_ is a _Fearless_ song, it is indeed a _Speak Now_ song, and a good one at that. Surprisingly, I’ve found I prefer _Long Live (Taylor’s Version)_ to the original. Now every time I listen to it, it reminds me of the Eras Tour.

I dislike _Sparks Fly (Taylor’s Version)_. The drop in the chorus isn’t as hard-hitting, and Taylor’s voice is lacking in energy. _Mean (Taylor’s Version)_ feels a little goofy; that is just plain and simple a song that is meant to be sung by young Taylor with a country accent. It pains me to say it, but I’m not a fan of _Dear John (Taylor’s Version)_. Partially because the production feels different, but also because the youth in Taylor’s voice in the original makes the song so much more impactful, given the lyrics.

This is probably a controversial opinion, but I hate _Enchanted (Taylor’s Version)_ with a passion. First of all, there’s a vocal glitch in the very first line. I don’t know if it’s an actual glitch in the mixing or just a bad vocal take, but something goes wrong when she says “there” in the line, _“there I was again tonight.”_ Once you hear it, you won’t be able to unhear it. Secondly, as with _Sparks Fly_, the drop in the chorus doesn’t hit nearly as hard; the guitar sounds muted to me. Finally, and this one pains me the most, she doesn’t do the breath at the end of the bridge. Everyone talks about the forgotten _Last Kiss_ shaky breath, but what about the _Enchanted_ breath? In the original, after the bridge, when she says, _“I was enchanted to meet you,”_ she takes an inward breath, as if catching it, before going into the iconic _“please don’t be in love with someone else.”_ In the Taylor’s Version, there is no inward breath, it just cuts to the next section. I know I probably sound deranged and obsessively nit-picky, but that has always been my favourite part of the song, and I have never heard anyone else ever talk about it.

The most controversial aspect of the _Speak Now_ re-recording was undoubtedly the _Better Than Revenge_ lyric change. In the original 2010 lyric, Taylor says: _“She’s better known for the things that she does on the mattress.”_ There was much debate about what Taylor was going to do. Was she going to change the slut-shaming lyric, or was she going to keep it as was? On release day, the new lyric was revealed: _“He was a moth to the flame, she was holding the matches.”_ I need to speak my truth: I love _Better Than Revenge (Taylor’s Version)_. The production is so much better. The electric guitar is going absolutely crazy, as is Taylor. She is giving it her all in her vocal delivery. My honest opinion about the lyric change? I don’t care. I really don’t.

I get why Taylor changed it. Since 2010, she’s experienced so much slut-shaming herself, so I understand why Taylor wouldn’t want to re-contribute to slut-shaming someone else. The new line is actually more cleverly written, but no one’s ready for that conversation yet. I love both versions of _Never Grow Up_; sometimes I want to listen to the innocent version sung by young Taylor, and sometimes I want to listen to the wistful version sung by grown up Taylor. Another song with two great versions is _Haunted_. The production hits so hard on the new version, but I do return to the original for nostalgia reasons from time to time. I’ve also included both versions of _Last Kiss_ on my playlist, because I do love the updated production on the new version, but nothing quite beats the emotion on the original, and yes, that shaky breath.

With _Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)_, we received six new vault tracks. I like the _Speak Now_ vault. It’s not quite at the level of the _Red_ or _1989_ vault, but it is still miles ahead of the _Fearless_ vault. The first track is _Electric Touch_, featuring Fallout Boy. Every real Swiftie knows _Speak Now_ is the rock album people beg for, so a Fallout Boy feature makes complete sense. This is a cute song about feeling nervous before a first date. Not a particular favourite of mine, but a cute song nonetheless. Speaking of cute, we then have _When Emma Falls in Love_. This is an adorable little song, and even though _“if Cleopatra grew up in a small town”_ is a slightly ridiculous line that makes me laugh every time, there are certain lines I absolutely love, like, _“She’s so New York when she’s in LA.”_

The next vault track is _I Can See You_. I always forget this song exists, but whenever I listen to it, I remember how fun it is. I love the electric guitar on this song. While a line like _“I could see you up against the wall with me”_ is hardly scandalous now in the wake of songs like _Dress, False God,_ and _Guilty as Sin?_, it was scandalous to imagine good girl fairy princess 19-year-old Taylor writing it. Although the _“then we kiss and you know I won’t ever tell”_ lyric from the bridge always makes me cringe, because something about the line delivery feels juvenile. _I Can See You_ is the only other vault track other than _All Too Well_ and _I Bet You Think About Me_ to receive a music video.

I don’t care if it has nothing to do with the actual song, I love this music video. Casting Taylor Lautner in it and letting him backflip all over the place was quite possibly the funniest thing she could have done. It was also cool of her to bring back Joey King and Presley Cash, who both acted in the _Mean_ music video when they were kids. But the best part of the video is getting to see Taylor back in her golden _Speak Now_ World Tour dress, wearing her iconic curls, with a ‘13’ on her hand and a handwritten lyric up her arm. Having “characters” from the Taylor Swift Universe break into a literal vault to free _Speak Now_ Taylor is a really fun and clever metaphor for Taylor reclaiming her work.

Then we have my favourite of the _Speak Now_ vault, _Castles Crumbling_, featuring Hayley Williams of Paramore. I adore this song. I love the production. The way Taylor’s voice breaks on the line _“used to chant my name now they’re screaming that they hate me, never wanted you to hate me”_ kills me every time. It saddens me knowing Taylor thought her career was ending back then; little did she know, it was just beginning. _Foolish One_ is another vault highlight. It is classic young Taylor. Taylor is nothing if not a hopeless romantic, and this song explores the downsides of wearing your heart on your sleeve. The final vault track is _Timeless_. Is this song a tad tone-deaf in its romanticisation of history? Maybe. But I love it. I find it to be cute and romantic, sue me.

Looking over the six _Speak Now_ vault tracks, I actually don’t think there’s any skips for me. It contains some hidden little gems, that’s for sure. _Speak Now_ is an album that is deeply special and important to me, both the original and _Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)_. It may not have been the most hyped up or commercially successful of the re-recordings, but it was the most exciting one to me.

![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uypS!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Facecebf9-f61b-4ec4-a5d1-b9efa94efa25_600x600.jpeg)![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6uJJ!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda2f8b29-9403-4682-8721-49208820162c_1400x1400.png)![Image 18](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!DYIc!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F492216b2-8b64-4b40-81fa-d121115f0f6c_600x600.jpeg)

On August 9th, during her last show of the first US leg of the Eras Tour in LA, the crowd lost their minds as Taylor slowly unveiled more and more blue outfits before announcing that _1989 (Taylor’s Version)_ would be out October 26th 2023. It was rather obvious throughout this era that Taylor knew _1989_ was her most commerically successful album. _1989 TV_ got things no other re-recording got. It was the only re-recording to get alternate covers. She also jazzed up the vault track title announcements by putting her fans’ detective skills to the test with a series of puzzles on Google.

Speaking of the _1989 TV_ cover, I was really curious to see how Taylor was going to possibly replace what is, in my opinion, her best album cover. Everything about the original cover is iconic; the polariod, the red lip, the seagull jumper, the fact that half her face is cut off. Despite not being better, I like the new _1989_ cover. She still gave it a white border, paying homage to the important role polaroid pictures played in the original era, she still incorporated seagulls, she’s still wearing a red lip, but most notably, she looks happier.

Like _Speak Now_, _1989_ got a full photoshoot. We must talk about the beachification of _1989_. Swifties couldn’t help but notice that for _1989 TV_, Taylor really leaned into a beach aesthetic. The entire photoshoot takes place on a beach, and the merch was beach themed. But the original _1989_ was never a beach album; it was a city album. More specifically, New York City, which is where the original photoshoot took place. So fans came up with the term “beachification” to describe Taylor’s rewriting of history. I’ve always found this discourse to be silly, because isn’t it obvious why Taylor did this? She did it to distinguish the _1989 (Taylor’s Version)_ era from the original _1989_ era.

Everyone always talks about the beachification of _1989_, but no one ever talks about the autumnification of _Red_ or the redification of _Reputation._ The original _Red_ photoshoot isn’t related to autumn in any way, people only associated that album with autumn because of the lyric from _All Too Well_, and Taylor leaned into it. Similarly, red was never a part of the colour scheme of the original _Reputation_ era, it was only until the black and red bodysuit on the Eras Tour came along. Real OGs remember that black and gold was the actual colour scheme of the album back in 2017. But I digress.

Taylor opens the _1989 TV_ foreword by talking about a haircut. A key aspect of the _1989_ album is that Taylor completely reinvented herself; she cut her hair off, moved from Nashville to New York, adopted a trendier fashion style, and started making pop music instead of country music. In the foreword, she says: “I was born in 1989, reinvented for the first time in 2014, and a part of me was reclaimed in 2023 with the re-release of this album I love so dearly. Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine the magic you would sprinkle on my life for so long (…) I present to you, with gratitude and wild wonder, my version of _1989_. It’s been waiting for you.”

The pop albums were always going to be the hardest to recreate, and _1989_ is proof of that. The synths in songs like _Welcome to New York, Blank Space, All You Had To Do Was Stay,_ and _How You Get The Girl_ just aren’t as punchy on the new versions. I’m sympathetic of _Shake it Off (Taylor’s Version)_, because you can tell she tried her best with it, but she was never going to be able to recreate that song, especially without Max Martin. I know people love the changes made to _I Know Places_, but I hate the robotic filter on her voice. Is the _“and we run!”_ vocal in the second pre-chorus better on the Taylor’s Version? Yes. But it’s not enough to save the song for me. I still prefer the original.

Unfortunately, it is time for us to discuss what are, perhaps, the two biggest screw-ups of the entire re-recording project: _New Romantics (Taylor’s Version)_, but even more so, _Style (Taylor’s Version)_. Just as she messed up the “weeEEE” in the chorus of _We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together TV_, she completely messed up the ahs in the leadup to the _New Romantics_ chorus. They’re quieter, for starters, and it somehow sounds like she’s hitting a different note. But it’s not just that one part; the production and vocal delivery on the original is, simply put, better.

But the crimes committed on _New Romantics_ pale in comparison to the atrocity that is _Style (Taylor’s Version)_. I refuse to go easy on her with this one, because how did that get green lit? First of all, that electric guitar. As soon as that opening riff begins, everything is wrong. Why does the guitar sound constipated? Everything about the production is off, some things are missing entirely. Taylor’s vocal delivery is also completely lacking in energy. If you want a detailed play-by-play of the differences in the instrumentations, I recommend watching this quick YouTube video:

I’ve since come to realise the reason why _Style TV_ is the way it is, is because perfection can’t be recreated.

But there are still certain songs on _1989 TV_ that are better than their original counterparts. Taylor and Jack Antonoff went absolutely crazy on _Out of the Woods (Taylor’s Version)_. They took an already incredible song and somehow made it even better. _This Love_ and _You Are in Love_ are two other examples where both the production and vocals are elevated in the new versions. The re-recorded song I was most scared about on this album was _Clean_, because it is my all-time favourite Taylor song. Surprisingly, however, I’ve found I prefer _Clean (Taylor’s Version)_ over the original now. The production is crunchier (in a good way) yet the vocals are clearer. Imogen Heap, I knew I could trust you. The tangerine vinyl variant includes the song Taylor made for the One Chance soundtrack, _Sweeter Than Fiction_, which Taylor is still yet to put on streaming.[8](https://afractionofmymind.substack.com/p/a-retrospective-of-the-taylors-version#footnote-8-164138642) I feel as if I’m the only Swiftie who actually likes that song.

The _Red_ vault may have some very high highs, but it also has some pretty low lows. The _1989_ vault, on the other hand, is more consistent in its highs. _“Slut!”_ subverted everyone’s expectations. Instead of being the upbeat feminist anthem everyone was expecting it to be, it’s a swoony love song about dating someone while the whole world is watching, but not caring, because you’re too drunk in love. This is a gorgeous song sonically. _Say Don’t Go_ is one of the weaker songs of the _1989_ vault, but a great song nonetheless, and incredibly catchy. The silence after _“I said, ‘I love you,’ you say nothing back”_ gets me every time, especially given the _“you’re not saying you’re in love with me, but you’re going to”_ line from the previous song.

_Now That We Don’t Talk_ is one of the shortest songs on Taylor’s entire discography, being only 2 minutes and 26 seconds long, but it does not disappoint in those 2 minutes and 26 seconds. I love Taylor’s low vocals on this track. It’s not an angry break-up song, per se, but she’s not yet above being petty, throwing out insults like, _“I don’t have to pretend I like acid rock, or that I’d like to be on a mega yacht with important men who think important thoughts.”_ _Suburban Legends_ is perhaps the weakest of the _1989_ vault, but not bad enough that I’d deem it a skip. Lyrically, this song is a bit confusing, with an odd simile here and there and a random high school reunion metaphor. But there are still some great one-liners, such as _“you were so magnetic it was almost obnoxious”_ and _“I broke my own heart ‘cause you were too polite to do it.”_

Finally, we have the crème de la crème of the vault tracks: _Is It Over Now?_. I cannot believe Taylor let this absolute masterpiece of a song gather dust on a hard drive all those years. I’m obsessed with everything about this song; the sassy, scathing lyrics, the gradual build sonically, the amount of lore references, from the snow mobile accident to the iconic blue dress on a boat incident. This is definitely up there as one of Taylor’s best bridges. It’s absolutely criminal this song didn’t get a music video.

Like _Red TV_, _1989 TV_ almost felt like its own era. This was the time Taylor was reaching her peak in popularity, mostly thanks to the Eras Tour, but also because of the re-release of her most popular album. Little did we know, _1989 (Taylor’s Version)_ would be the last re-recording era we would receive.

![Image 19](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZVbN!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7914b672-9486-4ba4-8ee3-ed79f86236d7_600x600.jpeg)![Image 20](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KZjr!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F43f05747-29a4-46fe-bedb-918a8e8813fd_1400x1400.png)![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IR5Y!,w_474,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F72b312fb-2cda-4a69-a9f2-d58209ab57dd_600x600.jpeg)

When Taylor announced she’d bought her masters, the biggest question remained: but what of Rep TV and Debut TV? I was absolutely gobsmacked to learn in Taylor’s letter that she hadn’t even finished recording a quarter of _Reputation (Taylor’s Version)_. But the more I’ve thought about it, the less it surprises me. I always knew of the six albums, _Reputation_ would be the hardest to recreate. The production on that record is so intricate and detailed, as is Taylor’s vocal performance. Nonetheless, as someone whose favourite album is _Reputation_, it was heartening to hear Taylor say she felt the original Rep era, both the music, videos, and photos, were already so good she felt she couldn’t improve upon them.

It’s no secret Swifties were going crazy with speculation about Rep TV. Every day was a new conspiracy. Everyone was convinced Taylor was saving the new Rep bodysuit and _I Did Something Bad_ as a surprise song on the Eras Tour for the _Reputation_ announcement. I still think that was the original plan, before she realised she wasn’t going to finish Rep before the tour concluded. We should have known when she both wore the gold bodysuid and performed IDSB that something was afoot. Personally, even as a Rep stan, I was always more concerned about the forgotten child, _Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)_. I am dying to hear songs like _Cold As You, Tied Together With a Smile, Should’ve Said No,_ and _Teardrops on My Guitar_ with Taylor’s mature vocals.

I was a Debutation Truther, not in the sense that I thought Taylor would ever do a double-drop (horrible idea), but in the sense that I loved pointing out the parallels between those records. The album covers _are_ quite similar; they’re the only covers she has where she is directly staring down the camera lens. Both are angsty records, although one contains a petty teenage angst, the other, a more mature and vengeful angst. Aesthetically, they are polar opposites. Debut is a bright summers day in a countryside paddock. _Reputation_ is a winter storm in the middle of a bustling city at midnight.

My prediction is that at some point, we will get an EP with just the _Reputation_ vault tracks. I think Taylor will hold off on releasing Debut TV until the 20th anniversary next year; I would love the symbolism of such a choice. In full honesty, I think Taylor is ready to move on from the Taylor’s Version project and has been for quite some time. I am personally still munching on _The Tortured Poets Department_, but there are geniune signs pointing towards TS12 coming sooner than we think. And let’s not forget Taylor still has a movie deal with Searchlight Pictures. No matter what happens, rest assured, I will be seated. I’m not sad we won’t be getting Rep TV. I was extremely nervous for it, especially considering how much I hated the snippet of _Look What You Made Me Do (Taylor’s Version)_. I recommend reading this Substack piece by Shelley-Marie on the snippet, where she summarises my thoughts perfectly:

One of the best things to come out of this Taylor’s Version project is the way it has opened up such an interesting conversation about ownership in art. Before Taylor publicly called out Scott and Scooter, the average music listener probably had no idea most of their favourite artists don’t actually own the music they make. That’s always been the norm in the music industry. A record label funds your music career; they pay for your studio sessions with producers, they pay to press the physical releases on CD and vinyl, they pay for publicity and book your interviews. That’s why being an independent artist is so much harder, because you have to pay for all of that out of your own pocket. But in exchange for those funds, most artists sign away the rights to their master recordings, which essentially means they sign away the rights to their work. Because the label own the rights, they have a certain level of control over their artists. They can weigh in and make decisions. They can cut songs from the album. And yes, if they want to, they can sell an artist’s masters, and they don’t need their permission to do so.

It’s not just the music industry that works this way. It’s very similar in the publishing industry. Most published authors don’t own the rights to their books. When they sign a book deal with a publishing company, similarly, the publishers pay for everything. In exchange, they get the rights, and usually, a large chunk of the profit. To someone who’s not a creative in any way, I understand why ownership may not seem like a big deal. But speaking as someone who is a creative: it is a big deal. And I’m fairly certain all artists would agree with me.

All art, whether it’s a song you’ve written, or a story you’ve written, or a painting, a video, a dance, anything of the sort — you are putting a piece of yourself into the art. Most of the time, the art is deeply personal to the creator. How symbolic that of all the musicians to happen to, it happens to the one who’s known for writing really personal songs; the one who’s known for opening up her diary and letting the world read it; the one who’s known for slitting her wrists and letting the blood run onto the page in the form of ink. To be clear, Taylor is not the first artist to lose her masters. She’s also not the first artist to re-record. But I think it’s fair to say she’s the first artist to really, truly succeed at re-recording.

While I’m not glad Taylor went through the experience of having her entire life’s work stolen from her, I have found this entire Taylor’s Version project to be extremely gratifying. It has been so much fun getting to go back and revisit her old catalogue, to see each album get its own time to shine in the sun again, and really be appreciated, especially considering when Taylor’s earlier albums came out the first time around, critics didn’t take her work seriously.

I am also extremely glad to have gotten the vault tracks. It’s crazy to think that without this endeavour, songs like _Mr Perfectly Fine, You All Over Me,_ Taylor’s version of _Better Man_, the 10 minute version of _All Too Well, Nothing New, Castles Crumbling, Foolish One, Slut!,_ _Is It Over Now?_ would still be buried deep in a computer file somewhere, never to see the light of day.

As much as I love the re-recordings, I am glad to be reunited with the original albums. While I love Taylor’s deep, rich, mature vocals we’ve gotten to hear from her as she’s reached her 30s, there is something so endearing about her baby voice that is present on her first four albums. But more than anything, I am happy for Taylor. I’m happy that after all this time, she finally gets to own what was rightfully hers all along. This entire project has had a major ripple effect across the music industry. I have a feeling it will become a cornerstone of Taylor’s legacy and artistry.

I can’t phrase it better than Taylor did herself: **“The best things that have ever been mine… finally actually are.”**

[![Image 22](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!29J9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9bbdd383-3295-4f74-bec0-e6ae0e3adfa9_1748x1240.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!29J9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9bbdd383-3295-4f74-bec0-e6ae0e3adfa9_1748x1240.png)

Everything is Taylor’s Version 🫶🫶

If you’ve somehow made it this far, thank you :)
