"**If This Was a Movie**" is a song by the American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") from the deluxe edition of her third studio album _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_ (2010). She wrote the track with [Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") and produced it with [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"). A fast-paced [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"), "If This Was a Movie" includes both acoustic and electric [string instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument"), drums, [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") notes, and full [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration"). In the lyrics, Swift's character begs an ex-lover to return to her and expects him to do so like it was a movie.

[Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") released "If This Was a Movie" digitally through the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") on November 8, 2011. The song reached charts in Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States, where it debuted within the top ten of the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). Two publication reviews of the track were published in late 2011; one found it engaging, and the other deemed that it showcased newfound maturity within Swift's lyrics. Retrospective rankings of [Swift's songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_songs_by_Taylor_Swift "List of songs by Taylor Swift") have included the track within the lower-tier positions.

On March 17, 2023, Swift released a [re-recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_/(music/) "Re-recording (music)") of the song, titled "**If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)**", alongside three other songs to [streaming services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") in celebration of the start of her [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour"), where she debuted it live on piano during a [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") show on June 23. The re-recording was also part of an effort to re-record her early catalog after a [dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") over the ownership of the [master recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recordings "Master recordings").

Background and release
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

[![Image 2: Martin Johnson wearing a black outfit with an electric guitar smiling](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg/250px-Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Martin-Johnson_blg.jpg)

[Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") co-wrote "If This Was a Movie".

[Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift") conceived her third studio album, _[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now "Speak Now")_ (2010), as a collection of tracks about the things she had wanted to say but was unable to do with the people she had met.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Conger-1) There were as many as 25 songs Swift wrote for the album,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Conger-1) which she co-produced with [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_/(record_producer/) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"),[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Pastorek-2010-2) who had worked on her previous releases.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-3) By around mid-2010, she had secured the final track list,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-4) where all the tracks were written by her.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Pastorek-2010-2) One exception, however, was "If This Was a Movie", which Swift wrote with [Martin Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Johnson_/(musician/) "Martin Johnson (musician)") alongside other songs.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)

"If This Was a Movie" was included as a [bonus track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonus_track "Bonus track") in _Speak Now_'s deluxe edition,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-6) which was released as a [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation")\-exclusive alongside the standard edition on October 25, 2010.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-7) [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") made the song digitally available, along with the other bonus tracks, through the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") on November 8, 2011.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpencer2013106-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-9) On June 23, 2023, Swift debuted the track live on piano during a show in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), as part of her [Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") (2023–2024).[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-10)

Produced by Swift and Chapman,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) "If This Was a Movie" is a [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock") [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad") that critics described as "somber" and "sparkling".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Lane-2023-12) Set on a fast pace,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) it has a length of 5 minutes and 48 seconds.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-13) According to the _[Seattle Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Weekly "Seattle Weekly")_'s Erin Thompson, the song has a basic arrangement and structure, which he regarded as "[Swiftian](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Swiftian "wikt:Swiftian")".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) It features acoustic [string instruments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_instrument "String instrument") from [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") and [folk music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music"), an electric guitar [amplified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_amplifier "Guitar amplifier") by [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distortion_/(music/) "Distortion (music)"), and full [orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orchestration "Orchestration").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) The [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") James E. Perone said that this arrangement could give "mixed-genre messages" to listeners.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) A simple, recurring guitar [riff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") is also played throughout,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) while drums and [key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") notes lead Swift.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) The [verse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_/(music/) "Verse (music)")'s melody is performed at a low [register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_register "Vocal register") and built on short [motive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motif_/(music/) "Motif (music)") [figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_/(music/) "Figure (music)").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) The dramatic [chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain "Refrain"),[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5) where Swift sings with a [twang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twang "Twang") accompanied by [harmonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony"),[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) [contrasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_/(music/) "Contrast (music)") the verse by being more melodious and performed at a higher register.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15)

In the lyrics, Swift's character pleads an ex-lover, who had left for six months, to come back to her, expecting him to do as such like it was a movie.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16) She imagines that through this perspective, he would be sorry to her for what mistake he made, and she would accept his apology and reconcile with him.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201741-15) A staff from _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_/(magazine/) "Billboard (magazine)")_ said that she was in a state of [coming of age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_of_age "Coming of age") in the lyrics, believing that she departs from the "fantasy world of high school" and examines "more mature content".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11) Swift on the song often recalls the important memories when they were together.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5) It also includes a lyric about being in the rain ("Stand in the rain/'Til I came out"), which Thompson felt was used extensively in her songs.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-17)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) By the conclusion, the ideal ending does not happen like Swift had hoped for.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202471-5)

In late 2011, two publication reviews of "If This Was a Movie" were issued. Thompson included it in the _Seattle Weekly_'s "Nice Hits!"—a [column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Column_/(periodical/) "Column (periodical)") that explores the best tracks out of the [top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_40 "Top 40") songs in a given time. He believed that while not "lyrically perfect", the track had the features that made Swift's songs engaging, including for what he considered vulnerable, relatable songwriting and a simple composition.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Thompson-2011-14) _Billboard_'s staff stated that it showcased "a more age-appropriate track" from her.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Billboard-2011-11)

Over the years, retrospective rankings of [Swift's songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_songs_by_Taylor_Swift "List of songs by Taylor Swift") have included "If This Was a Movie" within the lower-tier positions. _[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_/(magazine/) "Paste (magazine)")_'s ranking, published in February 2020, listed the track as 115th among her 158 songs—one of its writers Jane Song took issue with the line, "Come back to me like", which she heard as "Come back to me, daylight".[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-18) In her September 2020 ranking of Swift's 161 tracks for _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_, Hannah Mylrea placed the song at 150th, writing that "it stutters towards the finish line" and that it was "frustratingly repetitive" overall.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-19) [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") listed the track as 266th in his October 2025 ranking of her 286 songs for _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-20) The next month, Nate Jones of _[Vulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_/(website/) "Vulture (website)")_ updated his ranking of Swift's 245 tracks, where the song was placed at 170th; he viewed it as "the [mirror image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_image "Mirror image")" of her track "[White Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_/(Taylor_Swift_song/) "White Horse (Taylor Swift song)")" (2008) that, to him, made it "oddly superfluous".[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-21)

Carena Liptak of _[Taste of Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_of_Country "Taste of Country")_ included the song as 16th in her 2023 ranking of all 17 original tracks from _Speak Now_'s deluxe edition, saying that the song, while not among the album's most memorable, displayed "Swift's heartbreak songwriting at its wistful, [earworm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earworm "Earworm")\-y best" and that its emotional impact was skillfully handled. She attributed the placement to how other tracks better showcase Swift's "ability to wax poetic on heartbreak and nostalgia".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-22)

After its digital release in November 2011, "If This Was a Movie" debuted at number ten on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") chart in the United States, where the track also reached number three on [Digital Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Song_Sales "Digital Song Sales") with 163,000 [downloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2011-23) The top-ten entry on the Hot 100 made the song become the fourth track from _Speak Now_ to do so, in addition to extending Swift's record of most top-ten debuts for any act with ten.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2011-23) It peaked atop on [Country Digital Song Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Digital_Song_Sales "Country Digital Song Sales") as well.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-USCDSS-24) Elsewhere, the song reached number 191 in the United Kingdom[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UK-25) and number 17 in Canada,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaHot100-26) where it also peaked at number 10 on Canada Digital Song Sales.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaDSS-27)

"If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)"
----------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: \"If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)\"")\]

### Release and production

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Release and production")\]

To celebrate the start of the Eras Tour on March 17, 2023, Swift released a [re-recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_/(music/) "Re-recording (music)") of the song, titled "If This Was a Movie" (Taylor's Version)", on that day alongside three other songs to [streaming services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-30)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) The re-recording was also part of an attempt to re-record her early catalog after a [dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") over the ownership of the [master recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recordings "Master recordings").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-32) It has the same cover art as that of Swift's re-recorded album, _[Fearless (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_/(Taylor%27s_Version/) "Fearless (Taylor's Version)")_ (2021), and was included on the [compilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album "Compilation album"), _The More Fearless (Taylor's Version) Chapter_,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) which was also released on that day.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:2-33) Speculation ensued amongst fans regarding the song's release, according to some journalists, who questioned whether it would be featured on _Speak Now_'s re-recording, _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_/(Taylor%27s_Version/) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ (2023).[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-35)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Lane-2023-12) When the album's track list was unveiled on June 5, 2023, the song was not on it.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Sager-2023-34)

"If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)" has a length of 3 minutes and 57 seconds.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-36) _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")_'s [Will Hodgkinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Hodgkinson "Will Hodgkinson") described it as "straightforward, innocent, slightly breathy balladry with an orchestral backing".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16) The song was produced by Swift and its vocal engineer [Christopher Rowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Rowe_/(record_producer/) "Christopher Rowe (record producer)"). Musicians on the track were Amos Heller (who played bass), David Cook (piano), Matt Billingslea (drums and percussion), Max Bernstein (electric guitar), Mike Meadows (acoustic guitar), and Paul Sidoti (electric guitar); Bernstein also provided synthesizer [programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_/(music/) "Programming (music)"), while Meadows was the background vocalist. The [engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") were Bryce Bordone and Derek Garten, who was also the editor alongside Lowell Reynolds. David Payne was the recording engineer, assisted by Reynolds. The [mixer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixing_engineer "Mixing engineer") was [Serban Ghenea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serban_Ghenea "Serban Ghenea"), while the [mastering engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_engineer "Mastering engineer") was [Randy Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Merrill "Randy Merrill").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:2-33)

### Critical reception and chart performance

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=If_This_Was_a_Movie&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Critical reception and chart performance")\]

In two reviews of the four songs that were released right before the start of Swift's Eras Tour, "If This Was a Movie" (Taylor's Version)" received favorable comments. Writing for _[The Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Freeman_/(newspaper/) "The Freeman (newspaper)")_, Januar Junior Aguja said that the track could have new fans because of Swift's vocals on the re-recording, claiming that they had improved.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Aguja-2023-31) Hodgkinson wrote that the song was "corny but smart" and, to him, had Swift's early brilliance of "capturing an entire romantic drama in three minutes", considering that it had both an "[ingenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ing%C3%A9nue "Ingénue") spirit" and professionally-written ruthlessness.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)

Commercially, "If This Was a Movie (Taylor's Version)" reached number two on the [Bubbling Under Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbling_Under_Hot_100 "Bubbling Under Hot 100")[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-USBUH100-37) and number four on Digital Songs in the US with 11,300 downloads.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2023-38) On Country Digital Song Sales, it became her record-extending 19th number-one entry and made "If This Was a Movie" the first song to have two versions peak atop the chart.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-Trust-2023-38) On sales-component charts in other countries, the song reached number seven on Canada Digital Song Sales[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-CanadaDSS-27) and number thirteen on both [UK Singles Downloads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Downloads_Chart "UK Singles Downloads Chart") and [UK Singles Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Sales_Chart "UK Singles Sales Chart").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UKDownloads-39)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-UKSales-40) It also entered at number twelve on [Hot 40 Singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Aotearoa_Music_Charts#Hot_Singles_chart "Official Aotearoa Music Charts") in New Zealand.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie#cite_note-NZH40S-41)

Now (2010) | Fearless (Taylor's Version) \[2021\] Search for: “If This Was A Movie” is track sixteen on the deluxe edition of Taylor’s third studio album, _[Speak Now](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/albums/speak-now-album/)_ (2010). She wishes for a lost love to come back to her, like he would in a movie. The re-recorded version of the song, titled “If This Was A Movie (Taylor’s Version)” was released on March 17, 2023, and is featured on _The More [Fearless (Taylor’s Version)](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/re-recordings/fearless-taylors-version/) Chapter_ EP. ##### Table of Contents ### Background and Lyrical Theme Taylor wrote “If This Was A Movie” with Martin Johnson, who is the lead singer of the band Boys Like Girls. It is her only co-write on _Speak Now_. Previous collaborations between the pair include “[You’ll Always Find Your Way Back Home](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/work-for-other-artists/you-will-always-find-your-way-back-home/)” from the soundtrack of [_Hannah Montana: The Movie_](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/videography/filmography/hannah-montana-the-movie/) and the Boys Like Girls single “[Two Is Better Than One](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/features/two-is-better-than-one/).” A recurring guitar riff moves the song along, while its chorus features simple harmonies providing backup to Taylor’s signature twang. The lyrics suggest that she had gone through a breakup a few months earlier and still hopes things could go back to how they were before: _“I just want it back the way it was before/And I just wanna see you back at my front door.”_ ### Live Performance Taylor first performed “If This Was A Movie” during her sixth headlining concert tour, “[The Eras Tour](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/tours/taylor-swift-the-eras-tour/)” (2023-2024), almost 13 years after its release. It was the second surprise song during her show on June 23, 2023, in Minneapolis. She performed it acoustically on piano. ### Critical Reception “If This Was A Movie” was released on the deluxe edition of _Speak Now_ and was made a promotional single in November 2011. The song received positive reviews from music critics, with _Billboard_ rating it 4/5 stars. ### Taylor's Version Even though “If This Was A Movie” originally appeared as a deluxe track on _Speak Now,_ the re-recording of the song is featured as a track on the EP _The More Fearless (Taylor’s Version) Chapter_ (2023). It is worth noting that the song was the only track on _Speak Now_ not to be written solely by Taylor. Fans have speculated this might be the reason why it’s now being promoted as a [_Fearless_ _(Taylor’s Version)_](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/re-recordings/fearless-taylors-version/) song. [_Speak Now (Taylor’s Version)_](https://taylorswiftswitzerland.ch/index.php/re-recordings/speak-now-taylors-version/) would be, therefore, entirely written by Taylor alone. ### Lyrics **\[Verse 1\]** 9.content:
From teen country tracks to synth-pop anthems and rare covers, a comprehensive assessment of her one-of-a-kind songbook.

![Image 1: taylor swift 115 songs ranked list](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/lead_taylorswift-bb71d7be-f8ae-49c4-aec1-daa7b393510f.jpg?w=1401&h=788&crop=1)

Ranking all 237 of Taylor Swift's songs (from "Tim McGraw" to the 'Reputation' era, Rob Sheffield writes, "the weirdest and most fascinating thing about Taylor Swift will always be her music."

[Taylor Swift](https://www.rollingstone.com/artist/taylor-swift) the celebrity is such a magnet for attention, she can distract from Taylor Swift the artist. But Swift was a songwriter before she was a star, and she’ll be a songwriter long after she graduates from that racket. It’s in her music where she’s made her mark on history — as a performer, record-crafter, guitar hero and all-around pop mastermind, with songs that can leave you breathless or with a nasty scar. She was soaring on the level of the all-time greats before she was old enough to rent a car, with the crafty guile of a Carole King and the reckless heart of a Paul Westerberg — and she hasn’t exactly slowed down since then.

So with all due respect to Taylor the myth, the icon, the red-carpet tabloid staple, let’s celebrate the _real_ Taylor — the songwriter she was born to be. Let’s break it down: all 286 tunes, counted from the bottom to the top. The hits, the flops, the deep  cuts, the covers, from her raw 2006 debut as a teen country ingenue right up to _Midnights and The Life of a Showgirl._

Every fan would compile a different list—that’s the beauty of it. She’s got at least 5 or 6 dozen songs that seem to belong in her Top Ten. But they’re not ranked by popularity, sales or supposed celebrity quotient — just the level of Taylor genius on display, from the perspective of a fan who generally does not give a rat’s nads who the songs are “really” about. All that matters is whether they’re about you and me. (I guarantee you are a more fascinating human than the _Twilight_ guy, though I’m probably not.)

Since Taylor loves nothing more than causing chaos in our lives, she’s re-recording her albums, including the outtakes she left in the vault before. (_Reputation_ and her debut are the only ones she hasn’t released For the _Taylor’s Version_ remakes, both versions count as the same song. It’s a tribute to her fierce creative energy — in the past couple years she’s released an avalanche of new music, with more on the way. God help us all.

Sister Tay may be the last true rock star on the planet, making brilliant moves (or catastrophic gaffes, because that’s what rock stars do). These are the songs that sum up her wit, her empathy, her flair for emotional excess, her girls-to-the-front bravado, her urge to ransack every corner of pop history, her determination to turn any chorus into a ridiculous spectacle. So let’s step back from the image and pay homage to her one-of-a-kind songbook — because the weirdest and most fascinating thing about Taylor Swift will always be her music.

*   “Bad Blood” (2014)
    ------------------
    
    ![Image 2: Taylor Swift - Bad Blood](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/BadBlood.jpg?w=300)
    
    Melodically parched, lyrically unfinished, rhythmically clunky – this was a mighty strange pick for a single from an album as loaded as _1989_. There are a million things Taylor has in common with Paul McCartney – one is that celebrity grievances tend to sound like a penny-ante waste of their time, even when they’re totally understandable (unless you’re a fan of Macca’s “Dear Boy,” where John Lennon is his Katy Perry). The single remix is improved by Kendrick Lamar – but he wasn’t saving his A-game for this one.
    
    Best line: “Band-Aids don’t fix bullet holes.”
    
*   “Santa Baby” (2007)
    -------------------
    
    ![Image 3: Taylor Swift - Santa Baby](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SantaBaby.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Scott Gries/Getty Images
    
    Yes, she made a Christmas album, which is full of contenders for the basement of this list. But an oldie about a gold digger wooing Little Saint Nick was perhaps a dubious pick for a singer still in her teens.
    
    Best line: “I’ve been an awful good girl.”
    
*   “A Place in This World” (2006)
    ------------------------------
    
    ![Image 4: Taylor Swift41ST ANNUAL ACADEMY OF COUNTRY MUSIC AWARDS, LAS VEGAS, NEVADA, AMERICA - 23 MAY 2006](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/APlaceInThisWorld.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Picture Perfect/Shutterstock
    
    Apprentice work from the debut, when she was still learning the ropes as a country songwriter. Yet, the seeds of greatness are already there. Historical significance: This was the song where Tay discovered rain imagery, which in her hands was the equivalent of Sir Isaac Newton inventing calculus.
    
    Best line: “I’ll be strong/I’ll be wrong/Oh, but life goes on.”
    
*   “Christmas Must Be Something More” (2007)
    -----------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 5: Taylor Swift - Christmas Must Be Something More](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/ChristmasMustBe.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Peter Foley/EPA/Shutterstock
    
    A hymn about how Jesus is the reason for the season, with the hook, “So here’s to the birthday boy who saved our lives.” Unlike most boys Swift sings about, Jesus didn’t comment publicly.
    
    Best line: “What would happen if God never let it snow?”
    
*   “I’m Only Me When I’m With You” (2006)
    --------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 6: Taylor Swift - Only Me When I'm With You](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/OnlyMe.jpg?w=300)
    
    Could there be a less Swiftian sentiment? For better or worse, this girl is _always_ herself. That’s kinda the point.
    
    Best line: “I’m only up when you’re not down/Don’t wanna fly if you’re still on the ground.”
    
*   “Two Is Better Than One,” With Boys Like Girls (2009)
    -----------------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 7: Taylor Swift - Two Is Better Than One](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/BoysLikeGirls.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Bryan Bedder/Getty Images
    
    A long, long, very long duet with former Good Charlotte and Fall Out Boy tourmates Boys Like Girls, who are either from London or Nashville (they seem to switch accents at random). For some reason, they decided to delay her entrance until a minute into the song, arguably the worst decision in the history of decisions.
    
    Best line: “You already got me coming…undone.”
    
*   “Silent Night” (2007)
    ---------------------
    
    ![Image 8: Taylor Swift - Silent Night](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SilentNight.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Sipa/Shutterstock
    
    This bizarre version manages to miss almost every single note in the melody. They sure were in a rush to get this Christmas album out.
    
    Best line: “Shepherds quake at the sight.”
    
*   “Macavity” (2019)
    -----------------
    
    ![Image 9: taylor swift cats](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/taylor-swift-cats.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Universal Pictures
    
    This one will be tough to explain to future generations, but here goes: So they made this Hollywood movie out of the Broadway musical _Cats_. Full of magic, furry, singing cats. So much fur. So much magic. Taylor plus felines — it should add up to classic cinema, right? Not quite.
    
    Best line: “Macavity’s a mystery cat / He’s called the Hidden Paw.”
    
*   “Both of Us,” With B.o.B (2012)
    -------------------------------
    
    ![Image 10: Taylor Swift - Both Of Us](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/BothOfUs.jpg?w=300)
    
    Nice try at remaking “Airplanes,” but that Hayley Williams lightning does not strike twice.
    
    Best line: “Your money’s all gone, and you lose your whip.”
    
*   “The Last Time,” With Gary Lightbody (2012)
    -------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 11: Taylor Swift - The Last Time](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/TheLastTime.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Jonathan Hordle/Thames/Shutterstock
    
    Her duet with the guy from Snow Patrol. Unfortunately, their voices don’t mesh at all – what, is he auditioning for a Spandau Ballet tribute band? The funny moment is the _très_ Eighties synth-horn blurp at the three-minute mark.
    
    Best line: “This is the last time I’m asking you this/Put my name at the top of your list.”
    
*   “ME!” With Brendon Urie (2019)
    ------------------------------
    
    ![Image 12: Taylor Swift - ME!](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/ME.jpg?w=300)
    
    One of those beloved Taylor traditions: the Lead Single That Reveals Absolutely Nothing About the New Album. And for the second time in a row, it’s the weakest track by a mile. Honestly, Taylor would have released “Maxwell’s Silver Hammer” as the first single from _Abbey_ damn _Road_. “ME!” is her only song title with an exclamation point, an oddity for this most !!! of singers. Even Brendon Urie sounds squeamish, and he’s the guy who once released a song called “Folkin’ Around.” As we now know, she had “Cruel Summer” in the can, but opted not to make it the summer jam of 2019 because she decided to release “ME!” instead, a decision that will be studied by Swiftian scholars for years to come.
    
    Best line: “Hey kids, spelling is fun!”
    
*   “The Outside” (2006)
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 13: Taylor Swift - The Outside](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/TheOutside.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Winter/Getty Images
    
    Still a rookie, still learning, still trying to get away with “read between the lines” and “the road less traveled by” in the same verse.
    
    Best line: “Nothing seems to work the first few times/Am I right?”
    
*   ‘ThanK You AImee’ (2024)
    ------------------------
    
    ![Image 14: LONDON, ENGLAND - NOVEMBER 30: (EDITORIAL USE ONLY) (EXCLUSIVE COVERAGE) Taylor Swift attends the London premiere of "RENAISSANCE: A Film By Beyoncé" on November 30, 2023 in London, England. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/WireImage for Parkwood)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/taylor-swift-thank-you-alnee.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Mazur/WireImage
    
    This track is 4 minutes and 24 seconds long, and involves 5 different cello players. The letters “K,” “I,” and “M” are capitalized in the title, a reminder that there’s an excellent new Kim Gordon album. Sisyphus must appreciate the shout-out, but he’d probably rather roll a boulder uphill for all eternity than hear another song about this feud.
    
    Best line: “The blood was gushin’.”
    
*   “Hold On,” With Jack Ingram (2008)
    ----------------------------------
    
    ![Image 15: TWIN LAKES, USA - JULY 16:  ***EXCLUSIVE ACCESS*** Recording Artists Taylor Swift and Jack Ingram backstage at the 17th Annual Country Thunder USA music festival on July 16, 2009 in Twin Lakes, Wisconsin.  (Photo by Rick Diamond/Getty Images)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/taylor-swift-jack-ingram.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Rick Diamond/Getty Images
    
    An early country throwaway, released a decade later on Ingram’s [_From the Vault: Live 2007-2009_](https://clicks.trx-hub.com/xid/pmc_0aaa4_rollingstone?q=https%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F3nP3jcM%3Fasc_source%3Dweb%26asc_campaign%3Dweb%26asc_refurl%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fwww.rollingstone.com%252Fmusic%252Fmusic-lists%252Ftaylor-swift-songs-ranked-rob-sheffield-201800%252F&p=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rollingstone.com%2Fmusic%2Fmusic-lists%2Ftaylor-swift-songs-ranked-rob-sheffield-201800%2F&ref=pmcTrackonomicsReferrer&event_type=click). A teenage Swift chirps back-up harmony, doing the part originally sung by Sheryl Crow.
    
    Best line: “Sign our names in the dust on your family car.”
    
*   “Beautiful Ghosts” (2019)
    -------------------------
    
    ![Image 16: Taylor Swift - Beautiful Ghosts](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/BeautifulGhosts.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Universal Pictures
    
    She wrote this with Andrew Lloyd Webber for the [_Cats_ soundtrack](https://clicks.trx-hub.com/xid/pmc_0aaa4_rollingstone?q=https%3A%2F%2Famzn.to%2F35RYSHZ%3Fasc_source%3Dweb%26asc_campaign%3Dweb%26asc_refurl%3Dhttps%253A%252F%252Fwww.rollingstone.com%252Fmusic%252Fmusic-lists%252Ftaylor-swift-songs-ranked-rob-sheffield-201800%252F&p=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.rollingstone.com%2Fmusic%2Fmusic-lists%2Ftaylor-swift-songs-ranked-rob-sheffield-201800%2F&ref=pmcTrackonomicsReferrer&event_type=click) — as she said, “If you can’t get T.S. Eliot, get T.S.”
    
    Best line: “I watch from the dark, wait for my life to start / With no beauty in my memory.”
    
*   “Girl at Home” (2012)
    ---------------------
    
    ![Image 17: Taylor Swift - Girl At Home](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/GirlAtHome.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Evan Agostini/Invision/AP/Shutterstock
    
    A perfunctory cheating-is-bad homily, with barely any chorus.
    
    Best line: “I feel a responsibility/To do what’s upstanding and right.”
    
*   “Half of My Heart,” With John Mayer (2009)
    ------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 18: John Mayer and Taylor Swift - Half Of My Heart](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/HalfofmyHeart.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Amanda Schwab/Starpix/Shutterstock
    
    The real prize from his _Battle Studies_ album is “Heartbreak Warfare”; this is lesser J.M., with an underexploited T.S. cameo and an increasingly irritating premise of hearts having fingers, which they don’t. No wonder the girl in the dress cried the whole way home.
    
    Best line: “Half of my heart’s got a grip on the situation.”
    
*   “Sweeter Than Fiction” (2013)
    -----------------------------
    
    ![Image 19: Taylor Swift - Sweeter Than Fiction](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SweeterThanFiction.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Mike Strasinger/Admedia/Sipa/Shutterstock
    
    A warm-up for the synth-pop of _1989_, from the _One Chance_ soundtrack.
    
    Best line: “What a sight when the light came on.”
    
*   “Superman” (2010)
    -----------------
    
    ![Image 20: Taylor Swift - Superman](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Superman.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Matt Sayles/AP/Shutterstock
    
    A Lois Lane fantasy left off Speak Now, but it gets a real upgrade with her _Taylor’s Version_ vocal muscle.
    
    Best line: “Tall, dark and beautiful/He’s complicated, he’s irrational.”
    
*   “Cold as You” (2006)
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 21: Taylor Swift - Cold As You](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/ColdAsYou.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Ethan Miller/ACMA/Getty Images
    
    “I start a fight ’cause I need to feel something” – give her credit for honesty, even in this raw phase.
    
    Best line: “Every smile you fake is so condescending.”
    
*   “If This Was a Movie” (2010)
    ----------------------------
    
    ![Image 22: Taylor Swift - If This Was A Movie](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/IfThisWasAMovie.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Sipa/Shutterstock
    
    “Good evening, sir. May I help you? You’re a guy in a Taylor Swift song who wants to stand outside the window in the pouring rain, begging the love of your life to forgive your sorry ass? Take a number and get in line. No, _that_ line.”
    
    Best line: “But I take it all back now!”
    
*   “A Perfectly Good Heart” (2006)
    -------------------------------
    
    ![Image 23: Taylor Swift - A Perfectly Good Heart](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/PerfectlyGoodHeart.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Ethan Miller/Getty Images
    
    “It’s not unbroken anymore”? Paging the eminent cardiologist Dr. Toni Braxton.
    
    Best line: “Why would you wanna make the very first scar?/Why would you wanna break a perfectly good heart?”
    
*   “White Christmas” (2007)
    ------------------------
    
    ![Image 24: Taylor Swift - White Christmas](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/WhiteChristmas.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: George Napolitano/FilmMagic
    
    Unlike “Silent Night,” this was a yuletide carol she could handle, with a straight-down-the-middle country rendition.
    
    Best line: “Where the treetops glisten.”
    
*   “I Don’t Wanna Live Forever,” With Zayn Malik (2016)
    ----------------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 25: Taylor Swift - I Don't Wanna Live Forever](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/IDontWannaLiveForever.jpg?w=300)
    
    Neither she nor Zayn sound deeply interested in this dueling-falsettos battle from the _Fifty Shades Darker_ soundtrack. Maybe it works in the movie, but who wants to go find out? Really, they sound like two ghosts standing in the place of…sorry, sore subject, let’s drop it.
    
    Best line: “I’ve been looking sad in all the nicest places.”
    
*   “Mary’s Song (Oh My My)” (2006)
    -------------------------------
    
    ![Image 26: Taylor Swift - Marys Song](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/MarysSong.jpg?w=300)
    
    A through-the-years romance, with a sweet homespun touch.
    
    Best line: “I’ll be 87, you’ll be 89/I’ll still look at you like the stars that shine in the sky.”
    
*   “Highway Don’t Care,” With Tim McGraw and Keith Urban (2013)
    ------------------------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 27: Taylor Swift, Keith Urban and Tim McGraw - Highway Don't Care](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/HighwayDontCare.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Christopher Polk/Getty Images
    
    A duet from McGraw’s album _Two Lanes of Freedom_, with a guitar solo from Keith Urban. The plot: His ex is driving away, listening to a Taylor song on the radio, as Tay tries to coax the woman into turning the car around and going home. Perhaps McGraw’s finest duet since his great lost Nelly jam, “[Over and Over](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n3htOCjafTc).”
    
    Best line: “I bet you’re bending God’s ear talking ’bout me.”
    
*   “Change” (2008)
    ---------------
    
    ![Image 28: Taylor Swift - Change](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Change.jpg?w=300)
    
    Oh, the fall of 2008 – Chuck and Blair were still an item, Suede was killing it on _Project Runway_, and “Change” was a de facto victory song for Obama, complete with a thumbs-up for the “revolution.” Yeah, those were different times.
    
    Best line: “These walls that they put up to hold us back will fall down.”
    
*   “Nashville” (2011)
    ------------------
    
    ![Image 29: Taylor Swift - Nashville](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Nashville.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Shutterstock
    
    A cover of an obscurity by country singer David Mead, tucked away as a bonus on the Target edition of the _Speak Now Tour Live_ DVD.
    
    Best line: “Was that a blood or wine stain on your wedding dress?”
    
*   “Sweet Escape” (2011)
    ---------------------
    
    ![Image 30: Taylor Swift - Sweet Escape](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SweetEscape.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Shutterstock
    
    From the same live DVD, a remake of the Gwen Stefani solo hit. Taylor’s vocal sure fits the Gwen just-a-girl sensibility.
    
    Best line: “I must apologize for acting stank.”
    
*   “I Want You Back” (2010)
    ------------------------
    
    ![Image 31: Taylor Swift - I Want You Back](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/IWantYouBack.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Alex Berliner/BEI/Shutterstock
    
    A live acoustic tribute to the then-recently departed Michael Jackson, with a bit of Motown tremble in her voice.
    
    Best line: “Oh darling, I was blind to let you go.”
    
*   “Only the Young” (2019)
    -----------------------
    
    ![Image 32: Miss Americana](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/netflix-miss_americana-trailer-1920x1080-1.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Netflix
    
    “Only the Young” debuted in her excellent [doc _Miss Americana_](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/taylor-swift-miss-americana-lana-wilson-director-945678/), a synth-pop tribute to the next generation of political activists. It’s also a clever Swiftian fake-out, giving everyone a totally wrong idea of where she was headed musically — almost like she was announcing, “Nothing to see here, folks. Definitely no keepers left over from the _Lover_ era.” Was she already plotting to catch us off guard with _Folklore_? Don’t put it past her. But you’d never guess she was about to make an acoustic album full of folk songs about sweaters.
    
    Best line: “Up there’s the finish line / Our future is worth the fight.”
    
*   ‘I Hate It Here’ (2024)
    -----------------------
    
    ![Image 33: NEW YORK, NEW YORK - DECEMBER 14: Taylor Swift leaves The Box after celebrating her 34th birthday on December 14, 2023 in New York City. (Photo by James Devaney/GC Images)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/taylor-swift-i-hate-it-here.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: James Devaney/GC Images
    
    A tale of romanticism gone sour, with a precocious child grown into an alienated introvert who escapes to “the secret garden in my mind.” The 1830s line isn’t even the real verbal groaner in this song—that would be “if comfort is a construct,” which wins this album’s The Kind Under Where a Tree Has Grown award. But since “I Hate It Here” connects to “The Lakes,” it’s worth noting the 1830s sucked for Wordsworth and Coleridge.
    
    Best line: “I’ll save all my romanticism for my inner life.”
    
*   “I’d Lie” (2006)
    ----------------
    
    ![Image 34: Taylor Swift - I'd Lie](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/IdLie.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Ethan Miller/Getty Images
    
    A perky early throwaway about a teenage crush, recorded for her debut and briefly released as a bonus track.
    
    Best line: “He loves to argue, born on the 17th.”
    
*   “Umbrella” (2008)
    -----------------
    
    ![Image 35: Taylor Swift - Umbrella](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Umbrella.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Sipa/Shutterstock
    
    The Rihanna hit, briefly covered on the _Live from SoHo_ digital album. Her finest Ri tribute remains her 2011 version of “[Live Your Life](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eGgT8kV9QE8)” with T.I. onstage in Atlanta – sadly unreleased, but a duet that deserves to be enshrined for the ages.
    
    Best line: “Stand under my umbrella, ella, ella.”
    
*   “Look What You Made Me Do” (2017)
    ---------------------------------
    
    ![Image 36: Taylor Swift - Look What You Made Me Do](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/LookWhatYouMadeMeDo.jpg?w=300)
    
    The reason fans once cared about rap beefs: they inspired great songs, whether it was Queens vs. the Bronx (“The Bridge” vs. “The Bridge Is Over” vs. “Have a Nice Day”) or LL Cool J vs. Kool Moe Dee (“How Ya Like Me Now” vs. “Jack the Ripper” vs. “Let’s Go” vs. “To Da Break of Dawn”). But this just sounds like a trivial time-waster by her standards – Swift’s celebrity feuds are not really one of the hundred most interesting things about her. The main attraction is the retro Panic! at the Disco vibe. “Look What You Made Me Do” turned out to be the lamest track on _Reputation_, but an impressively perverse head fake – a lead single that ended up having nothing to do with the album, musically or conceptually, making sure her new relationship songs would come as a surprise. To find a comparable stunt, you might have to go back to 1982, when Michael Jackson fooled the world into thinking _Thriller_ was going to be a whole album of “The Girl Is Mine.”
    
    Best line: “It’s much better to face these kinds of things with a sense of poise and rationality.” Oh wait – that actually _is_ Panic! at the Disco.
    
*   “Paris” (2022)
    --------------
    
    ![Image 37: Taylor Swift](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/taylor-swift-paris.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Christopher Polk/Variety
    
    “I wanna brainwash you into loving me forever / I wanna transport you to somewhere the culture’s clever”—for Tay, that means a fantasy of Gay Paree. But the whole point of this song is that you can make your own Paris wherever you are, just by drawing your own dream map on the bedroom ceiling. And if you have an amour to share the dream with, all the better. “All the outfits were terrible, 2003 unbearable”—sounds like Taylor found somebody’s Friendster photo stash of crop tops and trucker hats. “Did you see the photos? / No, I didn’t, but thanks though” is being kind.
    
    Best line: “Privacy sign on the door and on my page and on the whole world / Romance is not dead if you keep it just yours.”
    
*   ‘CANCELLED’ (2025)
    ------------------
    
    ![Image 38: VANCOUVER, BRITISH COLUMBIA - DECEMBER 06: EDITORIAL USE ONLY. NO STANDALONE PUBLICATION USE (NO SPECIAL INTEREST OR SINGLE ARTIST PUBLICATION USE; NO BOOK USE). Taylor Swift performs onstage during "Taylor Swift | The Eras Tour" at BC Place on December 06, 2024 in Vancouver, British Columbia. (Photo by Kevin Winter/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/TS-song-list-showgirl-8.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Winter/TAS24/Getty Images
    
    If “Karma” is a cat, “CANCELLED!” is a squirle. She’s told this story countless times before, but almost always better, especially on _The Tortured Poets Department_, which makes you wonder if this is even a 2020s song or some still-unfinished _Rep_ outtake. (“Did you girlboss too close to the sun,” whew.) The Nineties indie-rock guitar intro and _Macbeth_ quote deserve a snazzier castle to call home.
    
    Best line: “You know who your friends are / They’re the ones with matching scars.”
    
*   ‘The Joker and the Queen,’ with Ed Sheeran (2022)
    -------------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 39: LOS ANGELES, CA - FEBRUARY 15:  Ed Sheeran and Taylor Swift attends The 58th GRAMMY Awards at Staples Center on February 15, 2016 in Los Angeles, California.  (Photo by Kevin Mazur/WireImage)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/taylor-swift-ed-sheeran-the-joker-and-the-queen.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Mazur/WireImage
    
    An Ed Sheeran ballad, refurbished into a sweet duet with his long-running favorite co-star. The video has the same actors who played Ed and Tay as little kids in the “Everything Has Changed” video — ten years later. Both singers sound right at home with the metaphor of a poker game — Ed can’t see it in her face, but she’s about to play her ace.
    
    Best line: “I’ve been played before, if you hadn’t guessed/So I kept my cards close to my foolproof vest.”
    
*   “September” (2018)
    ------------------
    
    ![Image 40: Taylor Swift - September](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/September.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Stephen Lovekin/Shutterstock
    
    The Earth, Wind & Fire classic, already covered by every wedding band on the planet, becomes a mournful banjo lament. It’s her tribute to the late great Maurice White, a songwriter who shared her knack for building hits out of quirky details. (Changing “the 21st night of September” to the 28th is a very Swiftian touch.) Next she might try “That’s the Way of the World” or “After the Love Has Gone.”
    
    Best line: “Love was changing the minds of pretenders.”
    
*   “Stay Beautiful” (2006)
    -----------------------
    
    ![Image 41: Taylor Swift - Stay Beautiful](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/StayBeautiful.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Rusty Russell/Getty Images
    
    An early stab at a take-the-high-road breakup song.
    
    Best line: “He whispers songs into my window.”
    
*   “End Game,” with Ed Sheeran & Future (2017)
    -------------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 42: Taylor Swift - End Game](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/EndGame.jpg?w=300)
    
    Future reaffirms her long-running bond with ATLien hip-hop, which goes back to her B.o.B. and T.I. duets. Plus her trusty wingman Ed Sheeran. She offers an update about her lipstick status (still red! good to know) and her relationship with drama: “I swear I don’t love the drama — it loves me!”
    
    Best line: “I bury hatchets, but I keep maps of where I put ‘em.”
    
*   “That’s When” (2021)
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 43: taylor swift fearless](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/taylor-swift-fearless-albums-chart.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: TAS Rights Managment\*
    
    A _Fearless_ outtake refurbished as a duet with her old friend Keith Urban. She pleads for forgiveness after crushing a lover’s heart for no particular reason, in the mode of “Back to December” or “Afterglow.”
    
    Best line: “I knew my words were hard to hear/And harder to ever take back.”
    
*   “The Way I Loved You” (2008)
    ----------------------------
    
    ![Image 44: Taylor Swift - The Way I Loved You](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/TheWayILovedYou.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Matt Sayles/AP/Shutterstock
    
    She meets a low-stress boy who doesn’t want love to be torture. Alas, this suitor is toast, because he reminds her how much she misses the manic pixie drama vampire she dated before. Sorry, dude – she loves the players, and she loves the game.
    
    Best line: “He respects my space/And never makes me wait.”
    
*   “Thug Story,” With T-Pain (2009)
    --------------------------------
    
    ![Image 45: Taylor Swift - Thug Story](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/ThugStory.jpg?w=300)
    
    The classic T-Pain and Taylor duet [from the 2009 CMT Awards](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rl00E4bdnQg), still T-Swizzle’s finest rap performance.
    
    Best line: “No, I never really been in a club/Still live with my parents, but I’m still a thug/I’m so gangsta you can find me baking cookies at night/You out clubbing, but I just made caramel delight.”
    
*   “I Wish You Would” (2014)
    -------------------------
    
    ![Image 46: Taylor Swift - I Wish You Would](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/IWishYouWould.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Todd Williamson/Invision/AP/Shutterstock
    
    One of her many, many songs set at 2 a.m. – clearly the most inspiring hour on Swift Standard Time – with a staccato disco guitar lick.
    
    Best line: “We’re a crooked love in a straight line down.”
    
*   “Big Star,” With Kenny Chesney (2017)
    -------------------------------------
    
    ![Image 47: Taylor Swift and Kenny Chesney - Big Star](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/BigStar.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Frederick Breedon IV/WireImage/Getty Images
    
    “This song is about a girl who had a dream and followed it,” Kenny Chesney tells the roaring Nashville crowd. One of those girls jumps onstage to sing along. “My friend Taylor Swift showed up on my birthday to surprise me,” Kenny explained. “In a lot of ways, that song and that lyric is Taylor’s journey.” Their touching “Big Star” duet came out on his concert album _Live from No Shoes Nation —_ 10 years after he gave this rookie a break as the opening act on his 2007 summer tour. There is no loyalty like Swift loyalty.
    
    Best line: “She signed autographs like she was Garth Brooks in a skirt.”
    
*   “Stay Stay Stay” (2012)
    -----------------------
    
    ![Image 48: Taylor Swift - Stay Stay Stay](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/StayStayStay.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: David Fisher/Shutterstock
    
    “Before you, I’d only dated self-indulgent takers” – but here she turns into a self-indulgent taker herself and (surprise!) she likes it, a phone-throwing nightmare dressed like a grocery-shopping daydream.
    
    Best line: “You came in wearing a football helmet and said, ‘Okay, let’s talk.'”
    
*   ‘Imgonnagetyouback’ (2024)
    --------------------------
    
    ![Image 49: RIO DE JANEIRO, BRAZIL - NOVEMBER 17: EDITORIAL USE ONLY. NO BOOK COVERS. Taylor Swift performs onstage during "Taylor Swift | The Eras Tour" at Estadio Olimpico Nilton Santos on November 17, 2023 in Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro. (Photo by Buda Mendes/TAS23/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management )](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/taylor-swift-imgonnagetyouback.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Buda Mendes/TAS23/Getty Images
    
    A catchy oddity that resembles Olivia Rodrigo’s “Get Him Back,” except Taylor does not meet this guy’s mom just to tell her her son sucks.
    
    Best line: “Once you fix your face, I’m going in.”
    
*   ‘Foolish One’ (2023)
    --------------------
    
    ![Image 50: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - MARCH 17: Editorial use only and no commercial use at any time.  No use on publication covers is permitted after August 9, 2023. Taylor Swift performs onstage for the opening night of "Taylor Swift | The Eras Tour" at State Farm Stadium on March 17, 2023 in Swift City, ERAzona (Glendale, Arizona). The city of Glendale, Arizona was ceremonially renamed to Swift City for March 17-18 in honor of The Eras Tour. (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management)](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/Foolish-One-Taylor-Swift.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images/TAS Rights Management
    
    Some of the _Speak Now_ vaulties sound like she’s already rehearsing for _Red_, but “Foolish One” feels totally _Fearless._ It’s a guileless country ballad about a girl learning to trust her instincts. Can you believe she went from this song to “Shake It Off” in four years? Talk about an upgrade in terms of Voices In My Head content. Love the way she wrote the hook “it’s delicate,” then decided to save that line until she could give it a song all its own. Like a lot of decisions she made in 2010, this was a prescient one.
    
    Best line: “When my head is on your shoulder / It starts thinking you’ll come around.”
    
*   “Message In a Bottle” (2021)
    ----------------------------
    
    ![Image 51: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 30: Taylor Swift performs onstage during the 36th Annual Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame Induction Ceremony at Rocket Mortgage Fieldhouse on October 30, 2021 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Michael Loccisano/Getty Images for The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame )](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/taylor-swift-message-in-a-bottle.jpg?w=300)
    
    Image Credit: Michael Loccisano/Getty Images
    
    The first song Swift wrote with Max Martin and Shellback — the day she met them. It makes sense she left “Message in a Bottle” off _Red_, since it sounds so similar to “22”— she chose the right one. But it sounds like she’s already stretching ahead to _1989_. “How is it in London?” sounds like a fresh take on the transatlantic rendezvous of “Come Back…Be Here.”
    
    Best line: “I became hypnotized by freckles and bright eyes, tongue-tied.”

Speak Now
=========

Speak Now Taylor Swift

By [Rob Sheffield](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/rob-sheffield/)

### [Rob Sheffield](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/rob-sheffield/)

[Contact Rob Sheffield on X](https://twitter.com/robsheff "X Icon")

*   [Why ‘Spinal Tap’ Is the Funniest, Most Emotionally Honest Movie Ever Made About Pop Music](https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-features/rob-reiner-spinal-tap-funniest-pop-music-movie-1235484606/)
*   [Backstage Bonds, Swiftie Support, and Tayvis Calls: 13 Things We Learned From ‘The End of an Era’](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/taylor-swift-the-end-of-an-era-doc-series-takeaways-1235482312/)
*   [Olivia Rodrigo Comes Alive!](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/olivia-rodrigo-live-at-glastonbury-review-1235478399/)

[View all posts by Rob Sheffield](https://www.rollingstone.com/author/rob-sheffield/)

October 26, 2010

![Image 2: Taylor Swift Speak Now](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif)

Matt Sayles/AP/Shutterstock

People like to fixate on [Taylor Swift](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/taylor-swift/)‘s youth, as if to say, yeah, she’s pretty good for her age. But that just begs a question: Where are all the older people who are supposedly making better pop records than Taylor Swift? There aren’t any. In a mere four years, the 20-year-old Nashville firecracker has put her name on three dozen or so of the smartest songs released by anyone in pop, rock or country.

Swift’s third album, _Speak Now_, is roughly twice as good as 2008’s _[Fearless](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-country/fearless-252671/)_, which was roughly twice as good as her 2006 debut. These 14 tunes chronicle the hopes and dreams of boy-crazy small-town Everygirls, and Swift wrote them all by herself. (She also co-produced _Speak Now_ with Nathan Chapman, who oversaw Swift’s first two albums.) Swift might be a clever Nashville pro who knows all the hitmaking tricks, but she’s also a high-strung, hyper-romantic gal with a melodramatic streak the size of the Atchafalaya Swamp. So she’s in a class by herself when it comes to turning all that romantic turmoil into great songs. At this point, she’s like the new [Morrissey](https://www.rollingstone.com/artist/morrissey), except with even more eyeliner.

Swift takes a step into adulthood with _Speak Now_ — she clearly aspires to the divorced-mom market where country stars do most of their business, slipping more grown-up details into her love stories. It’s tame by country-radio standards, but it’s still weird to hear T-Sweezy sing lines like “There’s a drawer of my things at your place.” Sometimes you can even tell what chick flicks Swift has been watching from the song titles: “Dear John,” “The Story of Us,” “Enchanted.”

In uptempo tunes like “Mine” and “Sparks Fly,” or ballads like “Back to December” and “Enchanted,” Swift’s voice is unaffected enough to mask how masterful she has become as a singer; she lowers her voice for the payoff lines in the classic mode of a shy girl trying to talk tough. Check the way she tosses off the “You made a rebel of a careless man’s careful daughter” part in “Mine.” Anyone else would have built the whole song around that, yet for Swift it’s just another brilliant throwaway detail. There’s a minimum of country schmaltz on _Speak Now_ — Swift likes her tempos fast and her choruses rock-size. In “Enchanted,” she even cops the Prince trick of duetting with her own filtered voice. ![Image 3](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2010/10/speaknow.jpg?w=820)

Editor’s picks
--------------

[![Image 4](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-albums-21st-century-1235177256/)

[![Image 5](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time](https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-lists/best-tv-episodes-of-all-time-1235090945/)

[![Image 6](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/best-albums-of-all-time-1062063/)

[![Image 7](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/themes/vip/pmc-rollingstone-2022/assets/public/lazyload-fallback.gif) ### 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century](https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-lists/best-movies-of-the-21st-century-1235200512/)

As for the boys she tangles with on _Speak Now_, they’re her usual type. “You’re an expert at sorry/And keeping lines blurry/And never impressed/By me acing your tests” — get used to that guy, Taylor, you’ll be meeting a lot of him. Her advice to these dudes for holding on to her? “Just keep on keeping your eyes on me,” she sings in “Sparks Fly.” And yet we can already tell this guy’s going to be long forgotten by the next song.

_Speak Now_ peaks with “Long Live,” a ridiculously over-the-top prom anthem with all the epic girl-group swoon of [the Ronettes](https://www.rollingstone.com/artist/the-ronettes) or [the Shirelles](https://www.rollingstone.com/artist/the-shirelles), plus a guitar hook from [Def Leppard](https://www.rollingstone.com/artist/def-leppard)‘s “Hysteria.” Swift belts about how getting crowned king and queen is the most excellent event that could ever happen. It’s the sort of prom song that could only come from an artist who chose to spend her high school years on a tour bus. Yet when Swift sings it, damn if you don’t believe every word.

_This story is from the November 11th, 2010 issue of Rolling Stone._
